Verified the code directly rather than taking the reviewer's word for it, and the accusation holds up — in fact the ground truth is worse than the reviewer stated.

app/api/chat/route.js:53-58 returns HTTP 403 with "AI Tutor requires a Pro subscription" to any signed-in user who is not premium/admin, and requires sign-in at all (401) before that. components/StudyApp.jsx:26-28 defines three tiers: FREE_TABS (learn-mode, content, notes, diagrams, practice), PREVIEW_TABS (flashcards, quiz, extras — preview then full paywall), and PREMIUM_TABS (mistakes, tutor — full paywall, no preview whatsoever). So 'tutor' gets zero free access, not even a taste. app/upgrade/page.js:21 sells "AI tutor" as a Pro-only monthly feature alongside evaluation chains and model answers.

Critically, the codebase itself already knows how to state this accurately elsewhere: app/economics/page.js:292 and app/business/page.js:287 both say verbatim "Notes are free. Flashcards, quizzes and AI tutor unlock with a subscription," and the same pages tag Notes "Free" and Flashcards/Quizzes/Tutor "Premium" in the UI (app/economics/page.js ~297-300, app/business/page.js ~297-300). That is a direct internal contradiction: the same product, in the same repo, correctly discloses that flashcards, quizzes AND the AI tutor are paid, while the Google snippet (app/page.js:6 and the duplicate at :9) lists "Notes, flashcards, quizzes, past papers and AI tutor" right after "Free interactive revision," with nothing to separate the paid items from the free ones. A reasonable reader — and Google, which surfaces this exact string as the search snippet — will read the list as an enumeration of what's included in the free offer, especially since the sentence structure gives no signal ("free notes, and quizzes with Pro" etc.) that a tier split exists.

I considered whether this is defensible as generic marketing puffery (a "loss-leader" framing, i.e., "free to start" language), or whether the reviewer misquoted a comment/dead code — but this is live, user- and Google-facing metadata (description and openGraph.description), not a comment or unused variable, and the same misleading phrasing is repeated near-verbatim across app/layout.js, app/ial-revision/page.js, app/economics/page.js and app/business/page.js meta descriptions, plus on-page CTAs. It is not an isolated slip; it's a systemic pattern that contradicts the site's own "What's included" sections. I could not find a reasonable counting rule or hidden context that rescues the claim — flashcards and quizzes are also not simply "free" (preview-only, then a hard paywall), which the reviewer didn't even flag. So I'm confirming the accusation rather than defaulting to defensible=true.

confirmed.quote: Every spec point is covered with concise, exam-focused notes, clear diagrams, and spaced-repetition flashcards that adapt to your strengths and weaknesses.
confirmed.whyWrong: Two parts are false. (1) Diagrams: all 20 Business sections have diagrams: 0 in the section inventory, and the Diagrams tab is Economics-only (StudyApp.jsx:34, subjects: ['economics']), so a Business student gets no diagrams anywhere. (2) 'Every spec point': the spec audit found sub-topic gaps in at least 15 sections — econ 4.3.5 role-state-macroeconomy is missing roughly three of its four spec sub-topics (no public expenditure, taxation, or public sector borrowing/debt content), bus 3.3.5 has no ratio analysis or HR metrics, bus 3.3.3 has no investment appraisal or contribution.
confirmed.groundTruth: audit/raw/section-index.json — diagrams = 0 for all 20 business sections; audit/raw/research-ial-spec-coverage.md section 1 'Coverage gaps are one level down (the numbered sub-topics inside each heading)'; ledger finding F114 'Business has zero diagrams across all … sections; the Diagrams tab (a free tab) is empty and Business Learn Mode never shows a diagram'
confirmed.fix: Every unit in the syllabus has a dedicated section, with concise exam-focused notes and spaced-repetition flashcards that adapt to your strengths and weaknesses — plus clear exam diagrams for every Economics topic (Business diagrams launching soon).
confirmed.defenceReasoning:
Verified both parts directly against the repo, not just the reviewer's citations.

(1) Diagrams: audit/raw/section-index.json confirms all 20 Business sections have diagrams:0 (business diagram total = 0 across the whole subject, vs 81 for Economics). components/StudyApp.jsx:34 confirms the Diagrams tab entry is `{ id: 'diagrams', ..., subjects: ['economics'] }`, and it's filtered out of `tabs` for Business users (line 247: `tabs = allTabs.filter(tab => !tab.subjects || tab.subjects.includes(activeSubject?.slug))`). I checked whether diagrams might exist elsewhere (embedded in notes/content as images/SVG) so the raw count could be misleading — they don't: Business content blocks only use types bullets/chain/def/fillin/flow/imp/link/mech/paragraph/reorder/subheading, no image/diagram type, and LearnModeTab.jsx builds its `diagramMap` straight from `sectionData.diagrams`, which is `[]` for every Business section, so Learn Mode's InlineDiagram never renders for Business either. Ledger finding F114 ('Business has zero diagrams across all ... sections; the Diagrams tab ... is empty and Business Learn Mode never shows a diagram') has status:'open' — a known, currently-unfixed defect, not a misreading. I also checked whether Business even needs diagrams (in case the omission were harmless): the spec audit notes IAL Business explicitly requires constructing labelled supply/demand diagrams, break-even charts, and decision trees, so this isn't a subject where diagrams are irrelevant to begin with. Net: a Business student — half the platform's stated audience — gets zero diagrams anywhere, contradicting 'clear diagrams' as a blanket platform feature.

(2) 'Every spec point is covered': the audit (research-ial-spec-coverage.md) does confirm one true, defensible fact — all 43 top-level spec headings (1.3.1-4.3.6 style) map 1:1 to app sections with correct numbering, none missing. If 'spec point' meant 'spec heading', the claim would hold. But that's not the natural reading in an exam-revision context: a 'spec point' conventionally means an individual assessable bullet inside the Pearson specification (e.g. 1.3.1.5c 'the role of financial markets'), and the audit itself frames it that way — 'coverage gaps are one level down (the numbered sub-topics inside each heading)' — before cataloguing sub-topic gaps in at least 15 of 43 sections, confirmed on direct inspection: econ 4.3.5 (missing public expenditure, taxation, public sector borrowing/debt — 'roughly three of four spec sub-topics... largest gap in the catalogue'), bus 3.3.5 (no ratio analysis/HR metrics), bus 3.3.3 (no investment appraisal/contribution/NPV/ARR). These are graded, examined sub-topics, not trivia. 'Every spec point is covered' is a specific, falsifiable factual claim (not vague puffery like 'the best'), made to students choosing a platform precisely because it promises full syllabus coverage — a material claim that is false under the reading a reasonable exam student would apply.

I also checked the 'not actually user-visible' escape hatch: the copy sits inside `<section className="sr-only">` in app/page.js, which is visually hidden from sighted users but is not dead code or a comment — it's live production markup read by screen-reader users and indexed by search engines as real SEO/marketing text, so it doesn't qualify as non-user-facing.

Conclusion: both prongs of the accusation survive scrutiny. The copy overclaims relative to verified, currently-open defects (F114 open in the ledger; sub-topic gaps confirmed directly in content-sections JSON and the spec audit). Severity is high rather than critical: this is an edtech revision site, not a safety/financial claim, and one component of the claim ('every spec heading has a section') actually is true, so it's a real but bounded misrepresentation rather than outright fabrication.

I opened every file the reviewer cited plus the surrounding code to check for an honest reading of "Revision PDFs — Download and print for offline revision" as a Pro-only benefit, and the accusation holds up completely.

1. No PDF-generation or print capability exists anywhere in the codebase: grep across app/, components/, lib/ for jsPDF, pdfmake, puppeteer, pdf-lib, pdfkit, window.print, and @media print returns nothing. There is no code path that turns app content into a downloadable/printable PDF.

This is a specific, falsifiable, itemized claim on the pricing/upgrade page — the highest-stakes place for this kind of error — and it's trivially disprovable by visiting /pdfs while logged out. I could not construct an honest defense.

confirmed.quote: Flashcards','Spaced repetition scheduled from your answers
confirmed.whyWrong: The Pro Flashcards tab does no scheduling. components/FlashcardsTab.jsx stores a per-card 'got-it' / 'not yet' status and rebuilds a round from the cards not yet marked 'got it' — there is no interval, ease factor or next-review date anywhere in it. The only real spaced-repetition scheduler (lib/spaced-repetition.js, SM-2 style with ease and intervals) is used by FlashcardsEngine at /flashcards-practice, which is completely free and has no premium gate.
confirmed.groundTruth: components/FlashcardsTab.jsx (statuses map + buildDeck rounds; zero references to nextReview/interval/ease) vs components/FlashcardsEngine.jsx:4 importing buildQueue/computeNextReview from lib/spaced-repetition.js on the ungated app/flashcards-practice/page.js; parallels ledger finding F086 (free Smart Practice vs paywalled Quiz tab)
confirmed.fix: ['Flashcards', 'Every card unlocked — the ones you miss come back next round until mastered']
confirmed.defenceReasoning:
I read both files directly rather than taking the reviewer's characterization on faith, and it holds up.

components/FlashcardsTab.jsx (the component actually rendered for the Pro-gated "Flashcards" tab in StudyApp.jsx — TABS lists it with `premium: true` at line 36, wired at StudyApp.jsx:735) tracks only a per-card string status ('got-it' / 'learning') in a `statuses` map. `buildDeck` filters cards down to those not marked 'got-it' and replays them as the next "round" (`startNextRound`). I grepped the whole file for interval/ease/nextReview/date-based logic — there is none. A card you get wrong reappears in the very next round, with no elapsing time, no increasing interval, and no per-card ease factor. This is a simple "drill until mastered" retry queue, not a memory-scheduling algorithm.

Meanwhile lib/spaced-repetition.js is explicitly headed "Spaced Repetition (SM-2) — Pure Functions" and implements real ease/interval/nextReview/repetitions math (createDefaultProgress, computeNextReview, buildQueue). This is imported only by components/FlashcardsEngine.jsx (line 4: `buildQueue, computeNextReview, createDefaultProgress`), which powers app/flashcards-practice/page.js. I checked that page and FlashcardsEngine.jsx for any subscription/isPro check — there is none; `isLoggedIn` only toggles Supabase sync vs localStorage, and the API routes (app/api/flashcards-practice/*) have no premium gate either. So the only real spaced-repetition scheduler in the codebase is on a completely free, ungated page.

That means the upgrade page's "Flashcards — Spaced repetition scheduled from your answers" bullet, sold as a Pro benefit, describes a real, specifically-named algorithm that exists in this exact codebase — just not in the feature being sold. The feature you actually pay for does something materially simpler and time-blind. This isn't loose puffery like "AI-powered" or "personalized"; "spaced repetition" is a well-defined, falsifiable technical term (SM-2/Anki-style expanding intervals), and the same engineering team already used that exact term precisely elsewhere in this repo for a different mechanism. I can't construct an honest reading where "scheduled from your answers" reasonably covers "reappears in the next immediate round with no time delay, ease, or interval." I also checked the ledger for precedent (F086: free Smart Practice vs paywalled Quiz, rated low/trust) — this case is worse because it's not just tier inconsistency, it's a specific advertised mechanism that the paid feature doesn't implement while a free page does.

confirmed.quote: Cancel in two clicks
confirmed.whyWrong: Cancelling takes far more than two clicks and does not finish on Revvy Learn at all. Settings → 'Cancel Subscription' opens CancelOfferModal, whose decline button is disabled until the student picks a reason from a required dropdown (CancelOfferModal.jsx:135, disabled={loading || !reason}); clicking 'No thanks, cancel my subscription' then calls handleManageSubscription, which redirects to the Stripe billing portal where the student still has to find and confirm the cancellation. That is a minimum of five interactions plus an off-site flow.
confirmed.groundTruth: components/SettingsPage.jsx:175-181 and :211-216 (onDecline → handleManageSubscription); components/SettingsPage.jsx:69-90 (portal redirect to Stripe); components/CancelOfferModal.jsx:113-138 (required reason select gating the decline button)
confirmed.fix:
Cancel anytime in Settings
No email, no phone call, no notice period — cancel yourself, finishing securely through Stripe.
confirmed.defenceReasoning:
I read the actual flow rather than taking the reviewer's word for it, and it checks out exactly as described, with the claim not even survivable under a generous counting rule.

app/upgrade/page.js:121 is live, user-facing marketing copy on the /upgrade route (not a comment or dead code) reading "Cancel in two clicks" with subtext "Settings → Cancel. No email, no waiting on a reply, no notice period."

Actual flow, traced through the cited files:
1. Settings page (components/SettingsPage.jsx:175-181): click "Cancel Subscription" -> opens CancelOfferModal (click 1).
2. CancelOfferModal.jsx:135: the decline button ("No thanks, cancel my subscription") is `disabled={loading || !reason}` — reason is bound to a `<select>` (lines 113-123) with a blank default option and `required`. The user must open the dropdown and pick one of seven reasons before the decline button is even clickable. That's a mandatory reason-gate, not an optional aside — at minimum one more click/selection, arguably two (open dropdown, pick option).
3. Click the now-enabled decline button (click ~2-3) -> SettingsPage.jsx:214-217 `onDecline` calls `handleManageSubscription`.
4. handleManageSubscription (SettingsPage.jsx:69-90) POSTs to /api/stripe/portal, which creates a Stripe billing-portal session (app/api/stripe/portal/route.js) and does `window.location.href = url` — a full off-site redirect to Stripe.
5. On Stripe's hosted portal the student still has to locate the cancel option and confirm it — interactions Revvy Learn's own code doesn't control and the copy never mentions.

So the subscription is not cancelled at all by the time the "two clicks" would be spent; the user has only reached a third-party page where the real cancellation still has to happen. There's no reasonable counting rule that gets to two: even generously not counting the dropdown-open as a separate click, it's Cancel Subscription (1) + pick a reason (mandatory, blocks the button) + Decline (2) + at least one more click on Stripe to actually cancel = a minimum of 3-4 required interactions, ending off-site. I checked for a second, click-count-friendly path (the separate "Manage Subscription" button that skips the modal) — but that isn't the path the copy describes ("Settings → Cancel"), and it still ends on Stripe's portal, not on Revvy Learn.

This isn't vague puffery like "hassle-free cancellation" that could flex under interpretation — "two clicks" is a specific, falsifiable operational claim, and it's false on the numbers alone, before even weighing the more serious problem the reviewer flagged: cancellation requires clearing a mandatory retention-survey gate and finishing on a platform Revvy Learn doesn't control. Given that subscription cancellation friction is a live regulatory hot topic (FTC click-to-cancel rule, UK auto-renewal rules) and this is a direct, quantified promise to the exact people trying to leave, I'm rating this higher than a typical copy nitpick.

confirmed.quote: Your first month is £1.
confirmed.whyWrong: The £1 first month is only applied to customers who have never had a subscription. The checkout route computes hadPreviousSubscription from currentSub.stripe_subscription_id and only attaches the intro coupon when it is false; everyone else goes to Stripe at the full £1.99. Any of the ~40 previously-cancelled subscribers who returns reads 'Your first month is £1', clicks 'Get Pro for £1 →', and is charged £1.99 with no warning.
confirmed.groundTruth: app/api/stripe/checkout/route.js:232-243 (const hadPreviousSubscription = !!currentSub?.stripe_subscription_id; coupon applied only if !hadPreviousSubscription); ledger finding F031 fix note 'pass trialEligible from /api/subscription and switch copy to "Subscribe" when false'
confirmed.fix:
Preferred fix (matches the already-planned F031 remediation — implement it rather than just patch the sentence): thread a `trialEligible` boolean from /api/subscription through to /upgrade, and render two honest variants instead of one universal claim:

- trialEligible === true (never subscribed): keep "Your first month is £1." / CTA "Get Pro for £1 →" — this is true for this audience.
- trialEligible === false (previously subscribed/cancelled): headline "Subscribe to Pro for £1.99/month." / subtext "Cancel anytime." / CTA "Subscribe to Pro →" — drop all £1 language for this segment since it will never apply to them.

If a same-day, no-personalization patch is needed first: stop stating the offer as universal. Change the H1 to "New subscribers get their first month for £1." and add a visible qualifier directly under the price, e.g. "£1 first month for new subscribers · £1.99/month after" — and change the CTA copy from "Get Pro for £1 →" to a neutral "See your price →" (or "Start Pro →") that isn't a specific price promise the checkout can silently break. This keeps the low-price hook for the audience it's true for while removing the unconditional, falsifiable claim from the CTA and headline seen by everyone.
confirmed.defenceReasoning:
Traced the full chain rather than taking either side's framing at face value.

Learn Mode (the app's own recommended 'START HERE' path), the section Quiz tab and the section Flashcards tab contribute nothing, so a student who has worked through every Learn Mode topic in Unit 1 opens /progress and sees 0% mastery, 0 streak and every topic red and labelled NEW. 'Track your mastery across all topics' is exactly what the page does not do.
confirmed.groundTruth: Finding F024 (app/api/progress/dashboard/route.js:48, severity high) — "Home 'Mastery', 'Streak', 'This Week' and /progress ignore Learn Mode, Quiz tab and Flashcards tab entirely"; supported by F023 (app/api/learn-mode/progress/route.js:37, Learn Mode's server write can never succeed). Confirmed in app/api/progress/dashboard/route.js:54-74, which reads only practice_question_progress.
confirmed.fix: Track your practice performance with detailed analytics and progress insights.
confirmed.defenceReasoning:
I read the cited files directly rather than taking the finding on faith, and the accusation holds up.

app/api/progress/dashboard/route.js:54-58 queries only `practice_question_progress`, and grepping the repo for who writes to that table shows exactly three writers: app/api/practice/progress/route.js (Smart Practice), app/api/flashcards-practice/progress/route.js (Flashcards Practice), and app/api/written-practice/progress/route.js. Two other real, server-persisted activities are excluded: the section Quiz tab writes to `user_quiz_attempts` (app/api/progress/quiz/route.js) and the section Flashcards tab writes to `user_flashcard_progress` (app/api/progress/flashcards/route.js) — neither table is ever read by the dashboard route. Learn Mode (components/LearnModeTab.jsx) persists completion state only in localStorage; its one server write path was already deleted (audit/PROGRESS.md packet 1: 'dead progress route deleted ... to close F023'), so today Learn Mode contributes nothing server-side, confirming F023's substance even though the specific file the reviewer cited (app/api/learn-mode/progress/route.js) no longer exists because it was removed, not fixed to work.

components/ProgressDashboard.jsx confirms the user-facing effect: `statusBadge()` returns 'NEW' whenever a section has zero rows in the queried data, with no hedging copy anywhere ('based on Smart Practice only', etc.) — just an unqualified 'OVERALL MASTERY' ring and 'DAY STREAK'. So a student who completes every Learn Mode topic in Unit 1, plus the section Quiz and Flashcards tabs (all real, saved, server-side progress), opens /progress and sees 0% mastery, a 0 streak, and every topic badged NEW. That is not a plausible-but-different counting rule — it is the literal, confirmed behavior.

I also checked whether the cited copy is actually user-visible, since app/progress/page.js:8 is a `<meta name="description">` tag, not on-page text — that would have been a legitimate 'not actually user-visible' defense. It doesn't work here: page.js:25 renders nearly identical text directly under the H1 ('Track your mastery across all topics'), so the same false claim is plainly on-screen, not buried in a meta tag or comment.

Nor is this ordinary puffery. 'Track your mastery across all topics with detailed analytics and progress insights' isn't a vague superlative like 'the best way to learn' — it is a literal, testable description of what a page named 'Learning Progress' is supposed to do, on a page whose entire purpose is that tracking. Testing it against the app's own recommended flow (Learn Mode is labeled 'RECOMMENDED · START HERE' in components/StudyApp.jsx) falsifies it directly. audit/PROGRESS.md lists packet 4 ('Progress and mastery truth') as 'not started', so this remains a live, unremediated gap as of today, not something already fixed elsewhere in the codebase.

I could not find a reasonable reading that rescues the claim, so per the default-to-defensible-only-when-uncertain instruction, I'm marking it indefensible rather than uncertain.

confirmed.quote: RETRIED
confirmed.whyWrong: Nothing was retried. The number under this label is results.filter(r => !r.correct).length — the count of questions answered wrongly, each seen exactly once. The label tells the student they had a second attempt they never got.
confirmed.groundTruth: components/practice/SessionSummary.jsx:7 (const totalRetried = results.filter(r => !r.correct).length); Finding F077 — "'RETRIED' stat counts questions that were never retried".
confirmed.fix: Replace the label "RETRIED" with "TO RETRY" (stat card at components/practice/SessionSummary.jsx:49). This keeps the same number (totalRetried, i.e. questions answered incorrectly) and preserves the product's real selling point — the spaced-repetition engine schedules missed questions to come back soon (computeNextReview resets nextReview to ~10 minutes out on a wrong answer) — without asserting a retry already took place in this session. If the design wants a plainer, non-promissory label instead, "INCORRECT" (parallel to the adjacent "CORRECT" stat) is the most literal and unambiguously accurate option.
confirmed.defenceReasoning:
Traced the full path, not just the cited line. SessionSummary.jsx:7 confirms totalRetried = results.filter(r => !r.correct).length. results comes from PracticeEngine.jsx's sessionResults state, appended once per handleAnswer call (line 495-502) against a fixed queue built once by buildQueue() in lib/spaced-repetition.js at session start (sessionSize=20, no re-insertion logic anywhere in buildQueue or handleAnswer). Each {sectionId, questionIndex} key appears at most once per queue because buildQueue iterates each question index once per section and either bucket (unseen/overdue) — there's no requeue-on-wrong step within a session. I checked for a same-session retry mechanism that might justify the label (the way components/fun/FunPage.jsx genuinely does, with its own retryPool that requeues wrong answers within the same play session) — but FunPage.jsx is an entirely separate feature (the 'Fun'/Blackjack quiz) and does not render SessionSummary at all. The Smart Practice Engine's SessionSummary has no such intra-session requeue. So within the session this label describes, a wrong answer is genuinely seen exactly once, confirming the reviewer's read of the ground truth.

I also checked the counterargument that computeNextReview() resets nextReview to ~10 minutes out on a wrong answer (lib/spaced-repetition.js:64), meaning the question WILL resurface in a future session — that's the real product behavior worth defending. But 'RETRIED' is past tense and asserts an event that already happened; the true state is 'flagged to retry later,' not 'retried.' The label also isn't gated to only overdue-requeued items — it counts every wrong answer in the session, including first-ever-seen questions, which by definition cannot have been 'retried.'

I confirmed the string is genuinely user-visible (not a comment, not dead code): it's the literal JSX text in the stat card, and app/globals.css:6188 only applies text-transform:uppercase/font styling — no content override. So none of the standard escape hatches apply: the number is not right under some other reasonable counting rule that matches 'retried,' the copy isn't a defensible marketing generality (it's a precise stat label sitting directly next to a number, parallel to 'CORRECT' and 'ANSWERED'), and it isn't quoting non-visible code. Per the instruction to default to defensible=true under genuine uncertainty, I still land on false here because there's no ambiguity in the trace — the finding is well-supported and a plausible true replacement is easy to state without losing the underlying selling point (adaptive spaced repetition will bring missed questions back).

confirmed.quote: MASTERED
confirmed.whyWrong: A topic is badged MASTERED once 70% of its items reach repetitions >= 3, so up to 30% of the bank can be untouched. 'Mastered' itself means three correct multiple-choice answers in a bank whose options are never shuffled and where 64% of correct answers are option B, with no confidence signal collected — a student who always picks B accumulates 'mastered' items they cannot actually answer.
confirmed.groundTruth: components/ProgressDashboard.jsx:63-69 (70% threshold) and app/api/progress/dashboard/route.js:69-73 (repetitions >= 3 = mastered); Finding F074 (components/practice/QuestionCard.jsx:94, severity critical) '64% of correct answers are option B; options are never shuffled anywhere'; Finding F076 (severity high) — 'a B-guesser accumulates "mastered" (repetitions>=3) cards they cannot actually answer'.
confirmed.fix: Until F074 (shuffle options / rebalance correct-answer distribution) and F076 (make a real confidence signal, or an unaided second exposure, a precondition for crediting repetitions) are fixed, don't badge any topic "MASTERED." Replace the label in statusBadge() with something that describes what is actually measured, not an outcome the data can't support: swap 'MASTERED' for 'ON TRACK' (or 'STRONG PROGRESS' if width allows), keep the same >=70% threshold and green color so the motivational/reward intent is preserved, and add a tooltip/subtext on the badge or ring: '70%+ answered correctly 3x in spaced review' so the claim is scoped to the actual mechanism instead of implying verified subject mastery. Reintroduce 'MASTERED' as copy only after the option-shuffle and confidence-gating fixes land, since at that point the underlying metric will actually support the word.
confirmed.defenceReasoning:
I read every file in the citation chain myself rather than trusting the reviewer's paraphrase, and it all checks out.

components/ProgressDashboard.jsx:63-69 — statusBadge() computes pct = mastered/total and returns {label: 'MASTERED'} once pct >= 70. Confirmed: up to 30% of a topic's items can be untouched (repetitions 0) while the topic still shows MASTERED.

app/api/progress/dashboard/route.js:69-73 — an item counts toward "mastered" the moment its practice_question_progress.repetitions >= 3. Confirmed exactly as cited.

components/practice/QuestionCard.jsx — renders {question.options?.map(...)} with zero shuffling logic; the option order is whatever the DB stores. I grepped every shuffle/sort/random call in the repo (ReviewMode, LearnModeTab, PreTest, FunPage, useBlackjack) and none of them touch an individual question's options array — they all shuffle which questions appear, never which position the correct answer sits in for a given question. So "options are never shuffled anywhere" holds for the actual answer-position bias claim.

I independently verified the 64% figure rather than taking the reviewer's or the ledger's word for it: walking every correctIndex in audit/snapshots/*.json (516 questions sampled) gives index 1 ("B") at 65.7% — matching the reviewer's "64%" almost exactly and matching the ledger's own F074 finding (severity critical, status open) which was derived the same way.

I then checked whether a confidence signal is actually collected in Smart Practice, since that's the linchpin of the "cannot actually answer" claim. lib/spaced-repetition.js and app/api/practice/progress/route.js do support a lastConfidence field, but components/PracticeEngine.jsx:466 calls computeNextReview(current, correct) with no third argument, and QuestionCard.jsx never renders a confidence prompt (unlike components/learn-mode/InlineQuiz.jsx, which has one). So in the actual Practice flow that feeds the dashboard's mastered/repetitions counts, no confidence is collected — confirmed. Ledger finding F076 (severity high, status open) independently states the identical scenario: "a B-guesser accumulates 'mastered' (repetitions>=3) cards they cannot actually answer."

So every load-bearing fact is accurate, not a misreading, not dead code, not a different-but-reasonable counting rule, and not something merely user-invisible — the MASTERED badge is the single most prominent artifact on the progress dashboard's per-topic bar chart and hero ring. This also isn't ordinary marketing puffery like "best-in-class" — it's an operational, falsifiable claim about the student's own recorded performance, and the team's own internal audit ledger has already scored the enabling bugs critical/high and left them open. A student who habitually picks 'B' when unsure (a common, non-malicious test-taking habit, not deliberate gaming) will accumulate MASTERED badges on real content they never engaged with, for roughly two-thirds of the bank. I could not construct an honest refutation; the closest defense ("it's just an internal algorithm label, like Anki's 'mature' cards") doesn't survive contact with the fact that the specific implementation is trivially satisfied by not reading the question at all, which is a materially stronger failure than ordinary spaced-repetition approximation error.

confirmed.quote: cards overdue
confirmed.whyWrong: The number is not a count of cards. The API counts every row in practice_question_progress with a past next_review — both flashcard rows (fc- prefixed) and Smart Practice multiple-choice questions — so the tile mixes two item types under one name. The same underlying rows are called 'questions' in the activity tooltip lower on the same page.
confirmed.groundTruth: app/api/progress/dashboard/route.js:148-154 (overdueCount loops all progressRows, no prefix filter) versus :64-66 (rows carry both bare and 'fc-' section ids); contradicted in-file by components/ProgressDashboard.jsx:255 (title={`${day.label}: ${day.count} questions`}).
confirmed.fix: Replace "cards overdue" with "items overdue" (or "reviews overdue," to echo the tile's own "DUE FOR REVIEW" caption). Both keep the urgency/selling intent intact while being accurate regardless of whether the overdue items are flashcards or Smart Practice questions. If product wants to keep the count split by type instead, that requires a code change (filter/report fc- vs bare rows separately), not just a copy edit.
confirmed.defenceReasoning:
I opened both files and the reviewer's read of the code is correct. In app/api/progress/dashboard/route.js: allProgress is fetched from practice_question_progress with no section_id filtering (lines 55-58); section_id values are either bare (Smart Practice MCQ rows, written by app/api/practice/progress/route.js) or 'fc-' prefixed (flashcard rows, written by app/api/flashcards-practice/progress/route.js — confirmed by that file's own comment 'Uses the same practice_question_progress table with fc- prefixed section IDs'). The overdueCount loop (lines 148-154) iterates progressRows with zero prefix discrimination, so it sums overdue flashcards and overdue Smart Practice questions together. ProgressDashboard.jsx:117 then labels that combined number 'cards overdue' under a 'DUE FOR REVIEW' stat tile — a real, user-visible string, not a comment or dead code.

I looked for a way to defend it and could not find one:
1. It isn't loose/generic SRS jargon in this codebase. Revvy Learn's own marketing pages draw a hard, repeated line between the two features: 'Flashcards' / 'Adaptive flashcard algorithm' (app/business/unit-*/page.js, app/upgrade/page.js) versus 'Smart Practice' / 'Questions adapt to you using spaced repetition' (app/practice/page.js). components/practice/QuestionCard.jsx is explicitly commented 'Smart Practice Engine' and its only user-facing microcopy calls its items 'question' ('This question will come back — spaced repetition'), never 'card'. So within this product's own established vocabulary, 'card' specifically means flashcard, not 'any spaced-repetition item.'
2. There's no alternate counting rule that makes 117's number a true card count — it is architecturally the sum of both row types, unfiltered.
3. The reviewer's contradiction citation holds up: ProgressDashboard.jsx:255 labels the same-shaped mixed practice_question_progress data 'questions' in the same file, which undercuts any claim that 'cards' is just casual, interchangeable phrasing — the component itself uses the precise term elsewhere.
4. HomeScreen.jsx:9 repeats the identical bug ('Review N overdue cards' from the same overdueCount), which shows this is a systemic mislabeling, not an isolated one-off word choice defensible as flourish.

Concrete failure mode: a student with 0 overdue flashcards but 12 overdue Smart Practice MCQs sees 'DUE FOR REVIEW: 12 — cards overdue,' opens Flashcards, finds nothing due, and reasonably concludes the app is broken or lying. That is a real user-facing accuracy problem, not a defensible marketing simplification — though it's a low-stakes, non-financial, non-legal claim on an authenticated personal-stats tile, so I'd rate it medium rather than critical/high.

confirmed.quote: Units 1 & 2 — AS Level
confirmed.whyWrong: 'AS Level' is UK GCE framing. On the Pearson Edexcel International qualification these students actually sit, Units 1 and 2 are the International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) units and the qualification is the International Advanced Subsidiary / International Advanced Level (IAS / IAL). Calling them 'AS Level' misnames the qualification on a site whose whole premise is IAL rather than UK A-level.
confirmed.groundTruth: audit/raw/econ_spec.txt:115-118 ('The Advanced Subsidiary can be claimed on completion of the International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) units') and :1989, :2001 (Unit 1 and Unit 2 both tagged 'IAS'); audit/raw/bus_spec.txt:101-103. Unit membership itself is correct — components/fun/constants.js:1-14 lists exactly the 6+6 Economics and 5+5 Business Unit 1-2 sections in audit/raw/section-index.json.
confirmed.fix: Units 1 & 2 — IAS (matches the term the spec itself uses for these units, and matches the 'Edexcel IAS' phrasing already used in components/TutorTab.jsx:249, so it's consistent with both the source qualification name and the rest of the codebase. If 'IAS' alone is judged too jargon-y for a first-time visitor, 'Units 1 & 2 — International AS' is the next-best short form — but avoid 'AS Level' unqualified, since econ_spec.txt itself uses that exact phrase for the separate UK-domestic qualification.)
confirmed.defenceReasoning: SubjectSelect.jsx:12,17 is genuine, rendered, user-facing UI copy (a button subtitle on the 'Choose Your Subject' game screen), not a comment or dead code. The cited source (audit/raw/econ_spec.txt:115-118, :1989, :2001) confirms Units 1-2 are International Advanced Subsidiary (IAS) units, and — critically — the spec itself uses the phrase 'AS Level' only to refer to the *different*, UK-domestic GCE qualification ('the equivalent AS and A Level qualifications taken in England and Wales', line 123), never to the IAL/IAS qualification these students sit. That is the opposite of a stretch reading by the reviewer; it's the source's own usage. Checking the rest of the repo for consistency (not just the cited file) makes it worse for the defense, not better: app/api/chat/route.js:95 explicitly tells the AI tutor 'This is the INTERNATIONAL qualification ..., NOT the domestic UK GCE'; components/TutorTab.jsx:249 already says 'Edexcel IAS'; app/layout.js metadata consistently says 'Edexcel IAL' / 'International A-Level'. So the product elsewhere is careful (even emphatic) about this exact distinction, and SubjectSelect.jsx is the outlier that uses the UK term. Unit membership (6+6 Econ, 5+5 Business) is correct and not disputed — only the qualification label is wrong. I looked for an honest refutation (dead code, reasonable alternate counting rule, ordinary puffery, reviewer misreading the source) and none holds up here; the copy names a checkable qualification incorrectly, using the term the primary source reserves for a different qualification, on a site whose core positioning is precisely 'IAL, not UK A-level.'

dismissed.quote: Every topic is mapped directly to the IAL syllabus, covering all four Economics units (WEC11, WEC12, WEC13, WEC14) and all four Business units (WBS11, WBS12, WBS13, WBS14).
dismissed.whyDismissed: The copy's claim is structural: every topic maps to an IAL syllabus heading and all four units per subject are represented. The audit cited by the reviewer confirms this itself, in section 1: "Result: NONE missing. All 43 app sections map 1:1 onto the spec's numbered headings, in the correct order and with the correct IAL numbering" (23 Economics headings across units 1-4, 20 Business headings across units 1-4). Section 5 of the same audit lists this as a "STRENGTH (do not change)": "Section list and numbering exactly match both IAL specs at heading level; no UK Theme numbering anywhere." The unit codes are conceded correct. The reviewer's examples (Merit/Demerit Goods, Alternative Views of Consumer and Producer Behaviour, The Accelerator Effect, Market Power as Market Failure, Core Competencies/VRIO) are extraneous GCE sub-blocks nested inside topics that do correctly map to real IAL headings (1.3.4, 1.3.5, 2.3.2, 3.3.5). That shows impure content within correctly-mapped topics, not topics that fail to map to the syllabus. The sentence never claims zero non-spec content or full sub-bullet completeness; it claims topic-to-syllabus mapping and four-unit coverage, both verified true by the audit and called a strength. The GCE-leftover content is a real, separate defect (tracked as F116) worth fixing in the product itself, but it does not make this specific marketing sentence false.

dismissed.quote: £23.88 a year on monthly · pays for itself in 6 months
dismissed.whyDismissed:
Verified both files directly. page.js:94-96 states the monthly plan's own standing/ongoing rate as "£1.99/month" (the £1 is explicitly labeled "first month" only — a one-time, disclosed introductory promo, not the plan's price). checkout/route.js:224-243 confirms the £1 intro coupon is a temporary acquisition incentive applied only to genuinely new customers on the first billing cycle; from month 2 onward every customer — intro or not — pays exactly £1.99/month indefinitely.

£23.88 = 12 × £1.99 is precisely the annualized cost of the monthly plan at its real, currently-charged standing rate — not a fabricated or padded reference figure. Comparing a lifetime/annual price against "12 × the regular recurring rate" (rather than a blended figure that folds in a one-time new-customer discount) is the near-universal convention across subscription marketing (Spotify, YouTube Premium, Substack, etc. all do this) — the intro price is a acquisition mechanic, not the product's price, and it's fully and prominently disclosed two lines above this exact copy, on the same screen, so there's no concealment. "Save 50%" (12/23.88 → 49.75%, rounds to 50%) and "pays for itself in 6 months" (12/1.99 = 6.03 months) both flow consistently from that same standing rate — internally coherent, not independently massaged.

The reviewer's recomputation is not wrong arithmetic, but it substitutes a different (and non-standard) reference basis — blending a one-time £1 promo into what is being presented as an annualized/ongoing-rate comparison — and calls the result "the" correct answer. That's a defensible alternative framing, not proof the published copy is false. Even judged against the reviewer's own intro-inclusive numbers, continuous elapsed breakeven works out to ~6.5 months, which is still fairly rounded by "6 months" in ordinary marketing language (nobody writes "6.03" or "6.53 months"). Given the standing-rate figures are truthful, verifiable against the page's own disclosed pricing, and consistent with standard industry practice, I could not honestly conclude this is a false claim — only that it uses a common, disclosed comparison convention the reviewer prefers not to use.

dismissed.quote: Quizzes with marking','Examiner-style feedback, not just right or wrong
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I read both cited files plus the actual quiz content (audit/snapshots/2026-09-11-post-packet-0__economics__price-determination.json, which holds the live q.explanation strings rendered by QuizTab.jsx:143-145).

The reviewer is right about the mechanism (MCQ scored against correctIndex; explanation is a static per-question string; AO-based marking lives only in the separate written-practice/evaluate route with its examiner AO1-AO4 system prompt) but wrong about what that mechanism produces, and wrong about what the copy claims.

1. "Quizzes with marking" - "marking" here is ordinary British-English usage for grading/scoring a quiz ("mark my homework," "get your test marked"), which is exactly what the feature does: it auto-scores every question, shows a score X/Y, persists best-score/attempt history via /api/progress/quiz, and visually marks each option correct/incorrect. Nothing in the bullet claims AO-based marking - that's a different bullet's territory (Evaluation chains/Model answers), and MCQs structurally can't carry AO3/AO4 marks anyway since there's no extended writing to analyse or evaluate. The reviewer is holding an MCQ feature to a written-answer marking standard that doesn't apply to it.

2. "Examiner-style feedback, not just right or wrong" - I pulled the actual explanation text the app renders, e.g.: "At equilibrium, Qd = Qs... Option B describes a disequilibrium situation... Option C is incorrect because... Option D is irrelevant to the definition of equilibrium." Every sample explanation follows this pattern: states why the correct answer is right, then walks through why each specific distractor is wrong. That is precisely the register of an Edexcel examiner's report (which explains why particular wrong options are attractive and why they're incorrect), not a bare checkmark/cross. The claim "not just right or wrong" is literally true - the UI shows a correct/incorrect highlight AND this reasoned paragraph, plus (for wrong answers) an "Ask Tutor to Explain" button for further personalised explanation. "Explanation is static/pre-written" doesn't disqualify it from being "examiner-style" - style refers to the register/content of the writing, not whether it's generated live per attempt.

The reviewer's citation of the Pro written-practice AO-marking endpoint is a red herring: that's a different, more advanced feature this bullet never references or implies. Nothing in "Quizzes with marking / Examiner-style feedback, not just right or wrong" promises AO breakdowns, mark schemes, or personalized commentary on the student's own wording - it promises more than a bare pass/fail on an MCQ, which the code demonstrably delivers.

This is defensible, accurate copy describing the actual QuizTab behavior, not a false claim about the separate written-practice marking feature.

dismissed.quote: Every spec point is readable without an account. Pro is the practice, not the content.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
The reviewer's accusation rests on a mismatched definition of "spec point." Throughout the entire codebase — not just this one line — "spec point" is the app's own established, countable term for the 43 top-level x.3.x spec headings (one app section per heading): app/economics/page.js says "4 units · 24 spec points," app/business/page.js says "4 units · 20 spec points," unit pages say "spec point by spec point," etc. The audit file the reviewer cites (audit/raw/research-ial-spec-coverage.md) itself uses a different, more granular vocabulary for the finer-grained items the reviewer is pointing to: it calls them "sub-topics," "numbered sub-topics," and "lettered bullets" (section 2 heading: "SUB-BULLETS MISSING INSIDE THE 3 SAMPLED SECTIONS"), and its own section 1 is titled "SPEC HEADINGS WITH NO SECTION." The audit's verdict on spec headings/points is unambiguous: "Result: NONE missing. All 43 app sections map 1:1 onto the spec's numbered headings, in the correct order and with the correct IAL numbering." That is exactly the claim the copy makes.

The gaps the reviewer lists (econ 4.3.5 missing sub-topics, bus 3.3.6 no contingency planning, bus 3.3.1 no PESTLE/Five Forces, econ 1.3.2 missing the six utility-maximisation reasons) are real per the audit, but they are gaps in sub-bullet depth within an existing, freely-readable spec-point section — not missing spec points. The copy never promises exhaustive sub-bullet coverage; it promises a free, accountless note for every spec point (heading), which is true and verified 43/43 by the reviewer's own source.

The "readable without an account" half is independently confirmed in code, not just asserted: components/StudyApp.jsx defines FREE_TABS = {'learn-mode','content','notes','diagrams','practice'} with no auth/sign-in check anywhere in that gating logic (grep for account/signIn/login/auth in the file returns nothing) — only flashcards/quiz/extras (preview) and mistakes/tutor (full paywall) are gated by isPremium. This applies uniformly across all 43 sections since gating is by tab type, not by section identity.

This is the reviewer applying a stricter, non-native reading of a term the product defines and uses consistently elsewhere, then treating an internal content-depth audit finding (sub-bullet gaps) as if it falsified a different, coarser-grained claim (heading/spec-point coverage). Given the source they cite affirmatively supports the copy's actual claim, and the access-control claim is independently verified in code, the line stands as accurate, ordinary marketing copy.

dismissed.quote: 4 8 20
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I opened both the file and the cited sources.

FILE (app/economics/unit-1/page.js:224-235): The three pills ("4", "8", "20") sit in a "Question types" row inside a compact "WEC11 at a glance" fact card, alongside rows for Exam paper, Duration, Total marks, % of A-Level, Data response, and Essay questions. There is no text anywhere claiming this is an exhaustive list of every mark tariff in the paper — it's a quick-glance snapshot, styled with three color-coded badges (blue/amber/purple per styles/landing.css:600-602).

Critically, the EXACT same three pills — "4", "8", "20" — appear verbatim and unchanged on all four unit pages (unit-1/WEC11, unit-2/WEC12, unit-3/WEC13, unit-4/WEC14; confirmed via grep). This is a shared, generic "at a glance" UI element, not a per-paper researched breakdown of every command word and tariff. That's strong evidence it's meant to illustrate the general shape of question sizes (short-answer, mid-length, essay), not to assert completeness.

SOURCE CHECK: audit/raw/research-ial-spec-coverage.md (the reviewer's own cited lines, 100-138) confirms WEC11 genuinely does contain 4-mark items (Section B short answers, Section C(c) Explain), 8-mark items (Section C(d) Examine), and 20-mark items (Section D Evaluate essay). So every number shown is a real, valid WEC11 tariff — none is fabricated.

The "Command-word tariffs" section in audit/README.md that the reviewer cites, and the specific lines 126-138 in the raw research file, are about a different and genuinely real bug: the practice[] question arrays elsewhere in the app (e.g. "Assess the usefulness of a PPF diagram... (10)", "Outline two assumptions... (4)") use command words and mark values (10-mark Assess, Outline) that don't exist anywhere in the IAL spec. That's the actual defect the audit flagged. This "Question types" snapshot pill row is a separate, unrelated UI element that uses only real, valid marks — it isn't part of the practice-question data structure the audit is describing at all.

So the reviewer has correctly identified a real problem in the source material (fabricated tariffs in practice questions) but mis-attributed it to this unrelated decorative snapshot, which contains no false values and makes no claim of completeness. Incompleteness (omitting 1, 2, 6, 14) is a legitimate UX/completeness critique, but it isn't a factual falsehood — nothing in the visible copy says "these are the only marks" or "the complete tariff set." That framing is the reviewer's own interpretation, not the copy's claim.

dismissed.quote: { letter: 'a', name: 'Types of Market Failure', kw: 'Externalities · public goods · information failure · merit/demerit goods' },
dismissed.whyDismissed:
Checked both sources directly.

1. econ_spec.txt (1.3.5, lines ~723-740): confirms the reviewer's grep — the literal strings "merit good" / "demerit good" never appear. The spec lists the five sources of market failure as externalities, the free-rider problem/non-provision of public goods, imperfect market information, moral hazard, and speculation and market bubbles.

2. app/economics/unit-1/page.js: the phrase "kw" fields at lines 73/77/86 are short keyword-teaser tags on a landing-page tile grid (see line 176: "Everything in Unit 1, spec point by spec point" / line 190-195: SECTIONS.subtopics.map rendering `st.kw` as a one-line keyword summary linking into the app). "Spec point by spec point" refers to the section-heading structure — and at that level the claim is verifiably true: all six subtopic tiles (1.3.5 a-f) map onto the spec's actual sub-bullets. Subtopic 'b' negative externalities, 'c' positive externalities, 'd' public goods/free-rider, 'e' information failure, 'f' moral hazard & bubbles — every one of the spec's five named sources of market failure is covered across b-f. Tile 'a' ("Types of Market Failure") is the overview tile, and its keyword line is a plain-English gloss, not a spec quotation.

3. Crucially, "merit/demerit goods" is not invented or off-topic content: audit/content-sections/economics__market-failure.json shows a full, real "Merit Goods & Demerit Goods" section (lines 496-658+) that explicitly ties the concept to information failure and externalities of consumption — which ARE the literal spec sources (1.3.5.1b "imperfect market information", 1.3.5.2c "external benefits/costs of consumption"). Merit/demerit goods is the conventional, decades-old textbook name economists use for exactly this phenomenon (underconsumption/overconsumption from information failure + consumption externalities); it is standard economics vocabulary, not fabricated or "wrong-subject" content, even though Pearson's spec PDF happens to describe the same idea without using that exact noun phrase.

4. This is a UI keyword tag, not a claim of verbatim spec text. No reasonable reader would take a 4-word comma-separated "kw" teaser under a topic tile as an assertion "these exact words appear in the Pearson specification document." The reviewer's own cited research doc (research-ial-spec-coverage.md) independently confirms the heading-level claim is accurate ("Strength: heading-level structure is exactly the IAL spec... 23 headings, 23 sections") — its complaint about merit/demerit is a curriculum-fidelity note for content writers (should the notes lean more on the spec's own phrasing?), not evidence the marketing copy is false.

Net: the reviewer is right that the literal string is absent from the spec PDF, but wrong to call this a false marketing claim — it's an accurate, ordinary content-summary label describing real, substantively correct material that maps onto genuine spec sources of market failure.

"Mastery across all spec points" reads the same way: it's saying the progress-tracking feature covers the whole spec, topic by topic — not that the Mastery percentage aggregates every learning modality (Learn Mode, Quiz tab, Flashcards, Smart Practice).

2) "Spec point" is the site's consistent house term for a syllabus/specification item, used identically dozens of times across the codebase (app/page.js, app/business/page.js, app/ial-revision/*, app/contact/page.js, etc.) — e.g. "Free notes for every spec point," "4 units · 24 spec points." It always means "syllabus topic," never "type of study activity." 3) Checked whether that breadth claim is literally true in the code: `app/api/progress/dashboard/route.js` builds `sectionStats` by looping `for (const id of sectionIds)` — i.e., over every section (spec point) in every unit in every subject — and returns a full subject→unit→section hierarchy with mastered/learning/new/total for each one. 4) I then checked the reviewer's own citation for accuracy. Finding #24 (index 23) says Mastery is computed "only from Smart Practice rows." That's imprecise: the dashboard aggregates `practice_question_progress`, which is written by BOTH the Smart Practice engine (`app/api/practice/progress`, plain section_id) AND the Flashcards tab (`app/api/flashcards-practice/progress`, `fc-`-prefixed section_id, explicitly merged back in the dashboard route via `originalId = row.section_id.replace(/^fc-/, '')`). So F024's underlying bug is real and verified — the Mastery *percentage* undercounts a Learn-Mode-only or Quiz-tab-only student — but that is a claim about which activities compute the score, which the audited copy never makes.

5) Conclusion: the reviewer is reading "all spec points" (topic breadth, confirmed true) as if it said "all learning modes" or "everything you do" (input-signal breadth, which is where the real bug lives). The copy under review does not assert the latter. This is the site's standard, consistently-used marketing shorthand for syllabus coverage, and it is accurate under that reading. F024 is a legitimate, separately-actionable product bug, but it does not falsify this specific line of copy.

dismissed.quote: Ask any Economics question
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I read both files directly.

app/api/chat/route.js:90-115 builds the tutor's system prompt dynamically per request from the section/unit passed in the request body:
```
const unitCode = unit?.code || '';
const isBusinessSubject = unitCode.startsWith('WBS');
const subjectName = isBusinessSubject ? 'Business' : 'Economics';
const system = `You are a tutor for the Edexcel International AS/A-Level (IAL) ${subjectName} specification. This is the INTERNATIONAL qualification (unit codes ${isBusinessSubject ? 'WBS11-WBS14' : 'WEC11-WEC12'}), NOT the domestic UK GCE.
Section: ${section?.number} — ${section?.title}
Unit: Unit ${unit?.number} — ${unit?.title} (${unitCode})
...
Focus on the content in this section. Use proper ${subjectName.toLowerCase()} terminology throughout.`
```
On the Unit 3 page this renders as: "...unit codes WEC11-WEC12... Section: 3.3.3 — Market Structures & Contestability. Unit: Unit 3 — Business Behaviour (WEC13)." So the prompt does contain a stale/incomplete range constant (WEC11-WEC12 instead of WEC11-WEC14) — that part of the reviewer's read is correct as a code fact, and it matches finding F018 in audit/raw/code-findings-flat.json ("Tutor system prompt has the wrong Economics unit range... Fix unit range to WEC11-WEC14").

But the accusation is that this makes "the tutor... told Unit 3 is not part of the qualification it covers," and that this falsifies the marketing line "Ask any Economics question." That doesn't hold up:

1. The same system prompt explicitly and unambiguously tells the model "Unit: Unit 3 — Business Behaviour (WEC13)" — it is never told Unit 3 is excluded. The WEC11-WEC12 fragment sits inside a clause contrasting IAL vs. UK GCE ("NOT the domestic UK GCE"), not a scope-restriction clause. Nothing in the prompt instructs the model to refuse or hedge on Unit 3/4 content; there's no code path that blocks or filters questions by unit at all.
2. "Focus on the content in this section" refers to the interpolated `section` variable (3.3.3, Market Structures) — ordinary pedagogical scoping ("stay on what the student is studying"), not a re-assertion of the WEC11-12 range. The reviewer is reading two independent template fragments as one restrictive instruction.
3. F018's own written impact statement (in the same audit file) never claims the tutor tells students a unit is out of scope; it says the tutor "cannot reference what the student just read and can confidently give advice that differs from the notes" — a content-injection/consistency bug, not a coverage-denial bug. The reviewer's specific "told Unit 3 is not covered" framing is an extrapolation beyond what even the finding they cite asserts.
4. The copy itself is unfalsifiable boilerplate, not a technical spec claim: "Ask any Economics question" is the identical AI-Tutor feature blurb reused verbatim on app/economics/unit-1, unit-2, unit-3, unit-4, and app/economics/page.js, with sibling variants elsewhere ("Ask any Business question," "Ask any globalisation question," "Ask any market failure question"). This is a template-level feature tagline describing an open-ended chat tutor (vs. a canned-FAQ box), which is exactly the kind of ordinary marketing hyperbole ("any question") that isn't read as a literal, precise guarantee about backend prompt constants.

So: F018 is a legitimate code-quality bug worth fixing in app/api/chat/route.js (the WEC11-12 constant should be WEC11-14), but it's an internal system-prompt accuracy issue, not a case where the user-facing tutor refuses or disclaims Unit 3 coverage, and it does not make "Ask any Economics question" false. The reviewer conflated a backend prompt-construction bug with a marketing-copy falsity claim.

Critically, I grepped every unit landing page and found the identical three pills — "4", "8", "20", same markup, same classes — hardcoded verbatim on all eight unit pages: Economics units 1-4 AND Business units 1-4 (app/economics/unit-1..4/page.js, app/business/unit-1..4/page.js). The audit's own source (research-ial-spec-coverage.md lines 131-148) documents that these units have genuinely different real tariff sets — e.g. Business command words are Define 2/Calculate 4/Construct 4/Explain 4/Analyse 6/Discuss 8/Assess 10-or-12/Evaluate 20 (no 14, no Examine), versus Economics' Define 2/Calculate 2-4/Draw 4/Explain 4/Analyse 6/Examine 8/Discuss 14/Evaluate 20. If this pill row were meant as a factual, paper-specific enumeration of command-word tariffs, it could not correctly be the same three numbers on all eight pages, since those units don't share a tariff set. The fact that it's a static, unchanging decoration — reinforced by a CSS palette hard-limited to exactly three fixed values — is strong evidence this is a generic "low/medium/high mark-weight" badge motif, not a data-driven or paper-specific breakdown of "the question types."

It's also not fabricated: 4, 8, and 20 marks are genuinely real, existing tariffs on the WEC14 paper per the reviewer's own cited source (Explain 4, Examine 8, Evaluate 20 all appear in the WEC13/WEC14 structure description). The label "Question types" next to three bare numbers, with no words like "all", "full breakdown", or "complete", reads as an at-a-glance sampler spanning short-answer to full-essay weight (a common UI shorthand: small/medium/large), not an audited, exhaustive command-word table — that job is done by the actual Learn Mode practice content, not a compact sidebar stat on a marketing landing page.

So: the reviewer is right that the pills omit 1, 2, 6, and 14, but wrong to treat this decorative, unit-agnostic UI badge as an assertion that "these are the paper's question types" (plural/exhaustive). Nothing in the surrounding copy claims completeness, and the reused-verbatim-across-8-pages pattern shows the component was never designed to be a per-paper authoritative listing. This is ordinary, defensible shorthand copy, not a factual misstatement.

Given the instruction to default to defensible=true under genuine uncertainty, and given the concrete evidence here (identical reuse across all 8 units + a CSS palette fixed to exactly 3 values) that this is decorative shorthand rather than a claimed-exhaustive fact, I find it defensible. Optional, non-blocking polish only: rename the row label from "Question types" to something unambiguous like "Mark range" or add a few more pills — but that is a UX clarity nicety, not a correction of a false claim.

It's true that econ_spec.txt lines 1824-1890 show Pearson's official 4.3.5 sub-topics are Public expenditure / Taxation / Public sector borrowing and debt / Macroeconomic policies, and that "merit" appears 0 times in the Edexcel IAL spec (IAL uses "information failure" framing instead of British "merit goods" terminology — confirmed by the research doc's own note). That is a real, separate finding: this app section, filed under spec code 4.3.5, teaches a different set of sub-topics than Pearson's official 4.3.5 does. But that is a curriculum-mapping/content-completeness defect (the section is mis-numbered or under-built relative to the syllabus), not a falsehood in this specific sentence of marketing copy. The copy never asserts "this matches Pearson's four official 4.3.5 sub-topics" or "this covers public expenditure/taxation/fiscal deficits/national debt" — it describes, accurately, what this section of the app actually teaches, which the student will see exactly as promised on click-through. Given the copy is directly verifiable against and matches the real content almost word-for-word, and the reviewer's true finding is about spec-code alignment rather than about this sentence being false, I'm calling this defensible. The underlying content/curriculum gap (3 of 4 real Pearson 4.3.5 sub-topics thin or absent in taught body text) is a legitimate, separate issue worth flagging for the content team, but it should not drive a rewrite of this line — that would fix the wrong artifact and risk producing new copy that's less accurate to what the section actually contains today.

dismissed.quote: Complete revision notes for Edexcel IAL Economics Unit 4 (WEC14). Globalisation, international trade, exchange rates, poverty and inequality, the role of the state, and economic development.

So the concepts the audit flags as "absent" are in fact taught and tested elsewhere in the section, just not in long-form paragraph prose.

[topic list]." is a verbatim template used across ALL FOUR unit pages (I checked unit-1, unit-2, unit-3, unit-4) — it's boilerplate SEO/meta-description phrasing naming the unit's syllabus headings, not a topic-by-topic, sub-bullet-by-sub-bullet completeness certification. "Complete" here reads naturally as "notes spanning the whole unit" (all six headings present, correctly ordered, correctly titled, each with real content) rather than "every single spec sub-bullet is covered verbatim" — the same way "Complete Guide to X" is standard, non-literal marketing usage in educational publishing.

Net: the specific copy at page.js:9 names a topic that genuinely exists, is correctly labeled, and has real substantive content across notes/quiz/flashcards/diagrams/practice. The reviewer overstates the case (misquotes the supporting lines, and treats "zero hits in prose" as "the topic isn't covered" when it's covered via other content types the audit didn't scan for this claim). This is defensible as ordinary marketing language describing unit-level topic coverage, not a falsifiable, specific claim that was disproven. dismissed.quote: Every {UNIT.code} point covered
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I read the file (app/economics/unit-4/page.js), the cited audit source (audit/raw/research-ial-spec-coverage.md), the finding at code-findings-flat.json #108 (0-indexed 107, "Unit 2 → Unit 3 cliff... Unit 4 sections are 2-3 steps total"), and audit/raw/section-index.json's six WEC14 rows.

The key question is what "point" means in "Every WEC14 point covered." This is not an isolated phrase — it's this codebase's own established term of art, used identically across 40+ instances site-wide: app/economics/page.js says Unit 4 economics has "6 spec points" and the whole subject has "24 spec points" (4 units × 6); app/business/page.js says Business has "20 spec points" (5+5+6+4). Those counts only work if "spec point" means the numbered top-level heading (4.3.1 through 4.3.6), not the lettered sub-bullets inside each heading (which would number in the dozens per unit, not 6). The unit-4 page itself lists exactly six such points (4.3.1–4.3.6) as SECTIONS, matching this convention.

Under that established, consistent definition, the audit's own top section is dispositive: "SPEC HEADINGS WITH NO SECTION... Result: NONE missing. All 43 app sections map 1:1 onto the spec's numbered headings, in the correct order and with the correct IAL numbering." For Economics Unit 4 specifically: "4.3.1-4.3.6 ... = 23 headings, 23 sections" (across all economics units) with titles matching verbatim (one minor title-wording variance noted, not a gap). Cross-checked against section-index.json: all six WEC14 rows (4.3.1–4.3.6) exist, each with real content (2-3 blocks, 4-6 subsections, 10-14 quiz questions, 3-5 diagrams, 18 flashcards, 3-5 notes) — none are empty or missing. So "every point covered," read the way this company consistently uses "point" everywhere else on the site, is literally true and the audit confirms it explicitly.

The reviewer's two citations are real but answer a different question:
1. research-ial-spec-coverage.md lines ~34/56 (the 4.3.5/4.3.6 sub-topic gaps, e.g., missing "public expenditure," "Lewis model," "capital flight," "tourism") is about depth within an existing, present section — a granular sub-bullet gap, not a missing spec point/heading. That's a legitimate content-quality defect worth fixing, but it doesn't make "every point [heading] covered" false; it's the difference between "this topic exists and has notes" (true) and "this topic's notes are as exhaustive as the full syllabus bullet list" (a stronger claim the copy doesn't make, and isn't how "point" is used anywhere else on the site).
2. Finding #108 (code-findings-flat.json, 0-indexed 107) is about pacing/engagement — "Unit 4 sections are 2-3 steps total" with no reorder/fillin widgets — confirmed by section-index.json's reorder:0/fillin:0 for all six WEC14 rows. But that's a UX/retention issue about how thin each lesson's interactive steps are, not a coverage claim; those same rows still show real quiz (10-14), practice (5), diagrams (3-5) and flashcards (18) content, so "zero recall widgets" is the auditor's narrower label for two specific widget types, not "nothing here."

Neither citation shows a missing spec point (heading); both show real, separate content-quality issues inside sections that do exist. Given the copy's own sitewide, self-consistent usage of "point" = numbered heading, and the audit's explicit heading-level confirmation of full coverage for Unit 4, this reads as ordinary and factually accurate marketing shorthand ("we cover the whole syllabus outline") rather than a claim that every lettered sub-bullet is drilled to full depth. The depth and engagement gaps the reviewer found are real and worth fixing in the product, but they don't falsify this specific copy under its established meaning.

dismissed.quote: Ask any Economics question
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I opened both cited sources.

app/api/chat/route.js:96 builds a system prompt: `This is the INTERNATIONAL qualification (unit codes ${isBusinessSubject ? 'WBS11-WBS14' : 'WEC11-WEC12'})...`. For Economics this hardcodes "WEC11-WEC12" instead of the correct "WEC11-WEC14" (confirmed correct range used everywhere else in the app: app/economics/page.js, app/economics/unit-4/page.js UNIT.code='WEC14', app/ial-revision pages, etc.). This is a real bug and matches audit/raw/code-findings-flat.json item #18 (0-indexed 17): "Tutor system prompt has the wrong Economics unit range, no section content, and contradicts the practice guidance..." (medium/trust).

But the reviewer's leap — "the tutor is told Unit 4 is outside the qualification" — doesn't hold up:

1. The very next lines of the same system prompt say `Unit: Unit ${unit?.number} — ${unit?.title} (${unitCode})`, which on the Unit 4 page renders as "Unit: Unit 4 — Developments in the Global Economy (WEC14)". So the model is explicitly told Unit 4/WEC14 is the current unit being tutored, in the same message. Nothing in the prompt says "refuse questions outside WEC11-WEC12" or "Unit 4 is out of scope" — there is no such sentence, and no code-level gate (no `if (unitCode not in range) reject`) anywhere in route.js. The wrong range is descriptive boilerplate about the overall qualification, not an instruction excluding Unit 4.
2. "Focus on the content in this section" refers to the current spec *section* (a sub-topic within whichever unit is loaded), not a restriction to units 1-2 — it appears identically regardless of which unit/section is passed in.
3. F018 itself (the cited finding) never claims the tutor refuses or restricts Unit 4 content. Its "impact" text is about a different problem entirely: Business students seeing Economics-flavored framing and the tutor lacking injected section content — not about Unit 4 exclusion. The reviewer is importing a claim the finding doesn't make.
4. "Ask any Economics question" is not unit-4-specific copy at all — it's identical shared microcopy reused verbatim on app/economics/unit-1, unit-2, unit-3, unit-4, and app/economics/page.js (and mirrored as "Ask any Business question" on all Business unit pages). It's a generic label for the AI Tutor feature's Q&A scope across the whole subject, not a claim about the internal correctness of a per-request system-prompt string.
5. Even granting the bug exists, it's a stray, contradicted line in a free-text LLM prompt (immediately followed by correct unit context) — not a functional access restriction. There's no demonstrated behavior where the tutor actually declines to answer Unit 4 questions; that would require testing, and the code contains no logic that would produce such a refusal.

The WEC11-WEC12 hardcoding is a legitimate code bug worth fixing (already correctly flagged as F018, a code-level fix: change the string to WEC11-WEC14), but it does not make the marketing microcopy "Ask any Economics question" false or misleading. Per the default-to-defensible rule and to avoid rewriting accurate, unrelated marketing copy based on a misapplied citation, this copy stands.

dismissed.quote: Mastery across all spec points
