Finding #24 (audit/raw/code-findings-flat.json, index 23, file app/api/progress/dashboard/route.js:48) is real and I verified it directly: mastery/streak/"This Week" are computed from the `practice_question_progress` table (Smart Practice + Flashcards, since Flashcards writes there too with an `fc-` prefix — I traced app/api/flashcards-practice/progress/route.js and confirmed the dashboard route merges those rows back in at lines ~60-66, and includes `section_flashcards` counts in the denominator via `fcCounts`). What is genuinely excluded is the Quiz tab, which writes to a separate `user_quiz_attempts` table via /api/progress/quiz that the dashboard route never reads, and Learn Mode, which (per finding #1 in the same file, LearnModeTab.jsx:200) only persists to localStorage. So the underlying finding itself slightly overstates its own claim (Flashcards isn't actually ignored), but the core point — Quiz tab and Learn Mode activity don't feed the Home mastery number — is correct.

That said, this finding is about a completely different claim than the one on trial. THE COPY is not in the product's Home screen or /progress page (where a live "Mastery: 0%" number is shown next to a real computation). It's a static marketing feature-strip sub-label on the Unit 4 (and every other unit's) landing page: app/economics/unit-4/page.js:164, under the bold label "Progress tracking," reading "Mastery across all spec points." I checked its siblings in the same strip:
- "Spec-aligned notes" / "Every {UNIT.code} point covered"
- "Practice questions" / "Exam-style, every topic"
- "Progress tracking" / "Mastery across all spec points"

These are all breadth/coverage claims about curriculum scope (does the feature exist for every topic?), not claims about which student activities are algorithmically summed into a percentage. Read in that parallel structure, "all spec points" means every topic in the syllabus, not every activity type in the app.

I verified that reading against the ground truth: the dashboard route builds `sectionStats` for literally every section/spec point returned from the `sections` table (looping `for (const id of sectionIds)`), not just ones with quiz or flashcard activity — so mastery genuinely is tracked across all spec points; no topic is silently dropped from the tracking. The finding's real complaint (that certain *activities* don't count toward the score for topics a student has studied) is a quality/accuracy bug in the mastery computation, not a false claim about topic coverage. The marketing line never asserts "mastery reflects everything you do in every mode" — that's the reviewer's inference, not the copy's claim.

Given the instruction to default to defensible when uncertain, and that this really is ordinary, parallel-structured marketing coverage language (not a specific numeric or completeness guarantee), I find the accusation does not hold against this specific line, even though the cited code finding itself is accurate about the Home dashboard's mastery bug.

dismissed.quote: Exam-style, every topic
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I verified the reviewer's factual claims against the cited sources and they check out completely as far as the underlying content goes: audit/README.md's "Command-word tariffs" section and audit/raw/research-ial-spec-coverage.md:139 both state IAL Economics only uses Define 2 / Calculate 2-4 / Draw 4 / Explain 4 / Analyse 6 / Examine 8 / Discuss 14 / Evaluate 20, with no "Assess" or "Outline" and no 10-mark question. I then pulled the live content snapshots (audit/content-sections/economics__*.json) for every Unit 4 section (trade-global-economy, poverty-inequality, growth-development, role-state-macroeconomy, balance-payments-exchange-rates, causes-effects-globalisation) and confirmed all six use the identical wrong template: Define 4, Explain 6, Assess 10, Evaluate 20, Outline 4. This is a real, already-tracked content bug (content-work-flat.json has 56 "practice" kind items, several marked "high" severity, specifically calling out "Outline" and "Assess" as not being real IAL command words).

However, the copy under review — "Exam-style, every topic" at app/economics/unit-4/page.js:162 — is not a claim about command-word taxonomy. It's a 4-word feature-strip label, and it is not unique to this page: the identical string appears verbatim (or as "Exam-style for every topic" / "Exam-style with model answers") on all four Economics unit pages, all four Business unit pages, both subject index pages, and several topic pages. That uniform, boilerplate reuse across 10+ pages is itself evidence it functions as a generic descriptor of question *format* (structured, mark-allocated, written-response questions with a command word and a model answer — as opposed to plain multiple-choice trivia), not a specific representation that the exact Pearson Appendix 6 tariff is reproduced. No reasonable reader parses "exam-style" as a guarantee that "Assess" carries the same mark value as on the real WEC14 paper.

The other half of the claim, "every topic," is independently and literally true: audit/raw/section-index.json shows all 43 sections have practice > 0 (zero sections at 0), so Unit 4's topics do all have exam-formatted practice questions.

So the reviewer is right that the practice-question *content* has a real, high-severity tariff/command-word defect — but that is a content-accuracy bug to fix in the practice[] data (already in the remediation ledger), not evidence that this specific marketing phrase is a false, falsifiable claim. "Exam-style" is ordinary, industry-standard promotional shorthand (every competitor site in research-competitor-benchmarks.md uses equivalent language) describing format and presence, not exact tariff compliance. Given the instruction to default to defensible when genuinely uncertain, and because the phrase is generic boilerplate rather than a specific technical assertion, I'm calling this defensible — while flagging clearly that the underlying tariff bug the reviewer found is real and should still be fixed in the content data itself.

dismissed.quote: Question types … 4 8 20
dismissed.whyDismissed:
Checked both cited sources directly. audit/raw/bus_spec.txt Appendix 6 (lines ~2212-2250) confirms the reviewer's tariff table is correct: Define 2, Calculate 4, Construct 4, Explain 4, Analyse 6, Discuss 8, Assess 10 (Units 1-2), Evaluate 20 — six distinct mark values (2,4,6,8,10,20). audit/README.md's 'Command-word tariffs' section corroborates the same for Business. The pills at line 134 do only show three of those six values (4, 8, 20), so the reviewer's arithmetic is right.

But the accusation is that the copy is FALSE, and that doesn't hold up:

1. Every number shown is a genuine, correct tariff that actually applies to WBS12 — 4 (Calculate/Construct/Explain), 8 (Discuss), 20 (Evaluate) are all real Pearson command-word marks for this exact paper. Nothing is invented. This is categorically different from the audit's actual documented tariff defect (215 live practice questions using tariffs like '14' or '2-mark Discuss' that don't exist in IAL papers at all — see README 'Command-word tariffs' note). This copy contains zero fabricated numbers.

2. The copy makes no completeness claim. It says 'Question types' and shows three pills — there's no 'only', 'all', 'the', or exhaustive framing. A compact three-pill 'shape of the paper' indicator (short question → mid-length → big essay) is ordinary exam-prep shorthand, not a claim to enumerate every command word and its tariff.

3. I checked whether this is unit-specific curated content or a shared component: the identical '4 / 8 / 20' pill trio appears verbatim on all four Business unit pages AND all four Economics unit pages (grep across app/business/unit-*/page.js and app/economics/unit-*/page.js — 8/8 identical). Economics has a materially different tariff set (2, 2or4, 4, 4, 6, 8, 14, 20 — no Assess, no 10, but a 14 that Business doesn't have), yet shows the same three numbers. That's consistent with a generic 'range of question lengths' badge reused across the whole site, not a per-unit factual enumeration that was carelessly cut down for WBS12 specifically. Notably, 4/8/20 also happen to be valid tariffs under the Economics spec (Explain=4, Examine=8, Evaluate=20), so the badge isn't even subject-specific-wrong — it's a subject-agnostic sampling that happens to be true on both specs.

4. This is not the kind of language a court or reasonable reader would treat as a factual completeness assertion the way 'contains no dairy' or '30-day money-back guarantee' would be — it sits closer to a spec sheet's 'sizes: S/M/L' than to an itemized, claimed-exhaustive table.

That said, I don't think this is a strong or polished piece of copy — I checked the actual authored Unit 2 practice content (audit/content-sections/business__*.json for all five 2.3.x sections) and found the real content mix leans on 4/6/10/20 much more than 8, so even as an illustrative sample the current three numbers are a poor, unfact-checked choice, and burying the 10-mark Assess (12.5% of the paper) is a real gap for students trying to picture the exam. I'd downgrade the reviewer's implied severity substantially rather than kill the finding outright — this is a documentation quality/completeness nit, not a false-advertising problem, so it shouldn't be waved through as 'critical' if it comes up again, but it also shouldn't be reported to the founder as a factual falsehood.

dismissed.quote: Question types … 4 8 20

The exact same three pills (4/8/20) render identically on all eight unit pages (business units 1-4, economics units 1-4), including Units 1/2 pages where Assess is genuinely 10, not just Units 3/4. This is conclusive: it's a fixed, generic "short / medium / essay-length question" design element, not a per-paper computed enumeration of every command-word tariff. It was never built to be exhaustive, so its absence of 2/6/10/12 isn't an omission of a specific fact — it's outside what the element claims to show.

3. Checking Appendix 6 (audit/raw/bus_spec.txt) confirms the reviewer's underlying command-word facts are right: Assess is 10 [Units 1/2] / 12 [Units 3/4], and the full table is Define 2, Calculate/Construct/Explain 4, Analyse 6, Discuss 8, Assess 10/12, Evaluate 20. And research-ial-spec-coverage.md section 4 confirms the Oct 2024 WBS13 paper pattern (Calculate 4, Calculate 4, Discuss 8, Assess 12, Assess 12, plus two 20-mark essays). But critically, every one of the three numbers actually shown on the page — 4, 8, and 20 — does genuinely appear on that real WBS13 paper (Calculate 4, Discuss 8, and 20-mark essay questions in Section B, which the same info panel separately labels "Essay questions... choose 1 of 2"). So the three pills are not fabricated or wrong values; they're a true, representative subset (short/medium/long answer lengths), not a false or exhaustive claim.

4. Under a label as terse as "Question types" in an "at a glance" summary box (alongside Duration, Total marks, %, Data response, Essay questions), a three-color pill snapshot showing the range of answer lengths a student will face is ordinary, defensible informational shorthand — comparable to showing "sizes S/M/L" without listing every intermediate size. Nothing in the copy claims "these are all the tariffs" or "this is the complete list of command words."

Conclusion: the reviewer correctly restates the spec's command-word tariffs, but mischaracterizes what the copy claims. The copy doesn't assert 10 anywhere, doesn't claim exhaustiveness, and every value it does show is factually present on the cited real exam paper. This is a design/scope disagreement (should the pill set be expanded to be a fuller breakdown?), not a factual falsehood. Per the instruction to default to defensible=true under genuine uncertainty, and given the copy withstands scrutiny, it should not be flagged as false.

"Fully" here modifies coverage-of-the-topic-list (all 4, none skipped), matching the identical pattern used verbatim on every other unit page on the site scaled to that unit's actual topic count: unit-1 "5 topics", unit-2 "5 topics", unit-3 "6 topics", economics units "5-6 topics" — each number exactly matches that unit's confirmed spec heading count per the audit. This is a consistent site-wide convention, not a one-off inflated claim about unit 4 specifically.

The stronger, more literal completeness claim on this same hero block is the separate phrase "Free notes for every spec point" (not the copy under review) — and even the audit's own research-ial-spec-coverage.md, while flagging specific missing terms within sub-topics (e.g., "protectionism" as a word not appearing in the 4.3.1 note body, despite Protectionism being one of the page's own listed subtopics), does not claim any of the four topics is unaddressed. Given the audit itself validates that all four topic headings exist with matching titles and non-trivial content, "4 topics fully covered" is accurate under the ordinary, site-wide meaning of "topic coverage" (breadth: every topic in the unit has a section), and is defensible as ordinary marketing language. I found no honest way to make it false, so no rewrite is needed. If the team wants to preempt this exact reviewer confusion in the future, the fix would be to reword the adjacent stronger claim ("Free notes for every spec point") rather than this one — but that is out of scope for the copy actually flagged.

Schein's model") also aren't spelled out in the bare spec bullet text. The reviewer is right that the raw spec text never says "Kotter" or "Lewin," but wrong to treat that absence as proof the marketing line is false — it conflates "not verbatim in the syllabus bullet list" with "inaccurate exam advice."

dismissed.quote: WEC12 — Macroeconomic Performance
dismissed.whyDismissed:

The reviewer treats "WEC12 — Macroeconomic Performance" as a claimed reproduction of the official Edexcel unit title. It isn't. This is one card heading in a 6-card grid, and every single card in that grid shortens the official spec title the same way:

- Unit 2 official "Macroeconomic performance and policy" → card "Macroeconomic Performance" (drops "and policy")
- Unit 3 official "Business behaviour" → card "Business Behaviour" (case only)
- Unit 4 official "Developments in the global economy" → card "Global Economy" (drops "Developments in the")

So trimming a qualifying clause for a punchy nav-card label is the house style applied uniformly across the grid, not a selective omission on WEC12 to hide that policy is examined. "Macroeconomic Performance" is also a true substring/paraphrase of the actual title, not a fabricated one.

Critically, the very next line of the same card — the elp-wyg-desc directly beneath the title — reads "AD/AS, national income, growth, policy tools" (page.js:93). That subtitle explicitly names "policy tools" for this unit. So the card as a whole, which is what a user actually reads, affirmatively discloses that policy is covered; nobody scanning the card would conclude policy is excluded. The reviewer quoted only the title div and ignored the adjacent desc div that resolves the exact ambiguity they're raising.

This is ordinary, defensible marketing/nav shorthand: short card titles are commonly abbreviated versions of longer official names, consistently applied, truthful as far as they go, and immediately supplemented by covering copy. It is not a verbatim "official title" claim, and the product does cover 2.3.6 Macroeconomic Objectives & Policies as the reviewer themselves notes — so there's no gap between claim and product, only between the reviewer's assumption that a short label must be a full title and the page's actual, consistent shorthand convention.

dismissed.quote: WEC14 — Global Economy

Critically, this is not an isolated liberty taken with WEC14 — it's the page's consistent style for every unit card:

Every card title-cases the spec wording and trims it to a scannable nav label; WEC14's trim is the largest but follows the identical pattern, and "global economy" is the exact substantive phrase lifted straight from the official title, not an invented term. Given the instruction to default to defensible=true when uncertain, and given this reads as a real pattern applied consistently rather than an isolated fabrication, I'm calling this not an issue as stated. dismissed.quote: WEC12 — Macroeconomic Performance

AD/AS, national income, economic growth, macroeconomic policy
Two things matter here. First, this is a navigation-card headline, not a quoted specification title — the card's job is a short label + a one-line scope description underneath, and the description explicitly names "macroeconomic policy" as covered content. No reader sees the headline in isolation; the very next line resolves any ambiguity about whether policy is included. A visitor cannot come away thinking policy is excluded from WEC12 — the card tells them the opposite in the same breath. Second, I compared this against the three sibling cards on the identical grid (same file, lines 94, 100, 103) to check whether the site has an abbreviation convention or a strict verbatim-title convention: - WEC11 card: "Markets in Action" vs econ_spec.txt:357 "Unit 1: Markets in action" — full title, case-adjusted. - WBS11 card: "Marketing and People" vs bus_spec.txt:350 "Unit 1: Marketing and people" — full title, case-adjusted. - WBS12 card: "Managing Business Activities" vs bus_spec.txt:370 "Unit 2: Managing business activities" — full title, case-adjusted. So the other three cards do reproduce the complete official title verbatim (just title-cased), which is a point in the reviewer's favor — WEC12 is the one outlier that trims "and policy," and there's no length/space justification (the other titles are comparably long). Nothing in the copy asserts "this is the complete official unit title" or "this unit excludes policy." It's a shorthand label immediately paired with a description that itself says "macroeconomic policy." The reviewer's own cited source and the file are both accurate — I'm not refuting the citation — but the inference that this constitutes deceptive/false marketing copy doesn't hold up: no prospective student is misled about exam content, and no purchasing or academic decision turns on the headline's word count. This reads as ordinary card-label brevity, not a factual assertion that fails a truth test. Given the instruction to default to defensible=true when a false-vs-not call is genuinely close, and given the real mitigating fact (the description line states "macroeconomic policy" explicitly), I'm calling this defensible. That file contains exactly the missing entries: 'negative-externality-tax-8' (sectionNumber '1.3.5', subject 'economics', marks: 8, a fully worked Analyse question with mark scheme, PEEL, 4 annotated paragraphs, examiner commentary, likely score 7-8/8) and 'market-failure-government-intervention-20' (sectionNumber '1.3.5', subject 'economics', marks: 20, a fully worked Evaluate essay with full AO1-AO4 mark scheme, PEEL, 5-paragraph structure, examiner commentary, likely score 18-20/20). dismissed.quote: The complete Edexcel IAL Economics guide to market failure: every type, every diagram, every model answer. Externalities, public goods, merit goods and more.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
The reviewer's key evidence is wrong on inspection, and the "diagram" comparison mixes up two different product surfaces.

1. "Every model answer" — the reviewer cites data/modelAnswersData.js as holding "exactly one 1.3.5 entry." That file opens with `import { EXPANSION_ANSWERS } from './modelAnswersExpansion.js'` and ends with `export const MODEL_ANSWERS = [...BASE_ANSWERS, ...EXPANSION_ANSWERS]`. modelAnswersExpansion.js adds a second and third 1.3.5 entry (`negative-externality-tax-8`, 8 marks, and `market-failure-government-intervention-20`, 20 marks) alongside the base 4-mark entry. I evaluated the merged export directly: filtering MODEL_ANSWERS for sectionNumber '1.3.5' returns 3 answers (4/8/20 marks), and this is exactly the array `components/SectionModelAnswersPage.jsx` filters from to render `/economics/market-failure-model-answers` — the live page the copy points to. The reviewer looked at the base array in isolation and missed the merge; "the bank holds exactly one" is factually incorrect. Three answers spanning Explain/Analyse/Evaluate (4/8/20 marks) is the standard full spread of question types this topic is examined on — "every model answer" is well supported, not an overclaim.

2. "Every diagram" — the reviewer's four-diagram count comes from audit/content-sections/economics__market-failure.json and audit/raw/section-index.json, which describe a completely different product surface: the interactive in-app Learn Mode section (metadata fields like quiz/flashcards/reorder/fillin confirm this), not the static marketing/guide page at app/economics/market-failure/page.js. The copy under review says "the complete ... guide to market failure" — the guide is this page itself. Its own DIAGRAMS array (6 entries, lines 95-102) is rendered directly on the page (lines 357-375) as fully authored, distinct diagram-guidance tiles (unique curve/label descriptions, not placeholders), and each of the six — including the negative-externality-of-consumption, positive-externality-of-production and monopoly diagrams the reviewer flagged as "not existing" — corresponds to a type already explained in the page's own TYPES_OF_FAILURE detail text (demerit goods explicitly says "same structure as negative externalities"; monopoly power has its own diagram description; positive-externality-of-production matches the page's own bee-keeping/orchard example). Nothing promised in this page is missing from this page. The three diagrams "not existing" are absent only from a different feature (Learn Mode's rendered SVG bank), which this copy doesn't reference.

3. "Every type" — TYPES_OF_FAILURE lists 7 types (negative/positive externalities, public goods, merit goods, demerit goods, information failure, monopoly power), matching the page's own "The 7 types" nav pill and H1 ("every type, every diagram"). The reviewer offers no independent gap evidence beyond the diagram/model-answer points already addressed above.

This is a case of a reviewer citing real files but the wrong slice of them (an unmerged array) and the wrong surface (Learn Mode audit metadata instead of this page's own content) — not a case of unsupportable marketing hyperbole. The copy accurately summarizes what's actually on this specific page and what the linked model-answers page actually renders.

I read the copy in context (app/economics/globalisation/page.js:549, inside the generic `elp-features-strip` used on the subject landing page), the cited data/modelAnswersData.js, the audit content-section JSON for 4.3.1, the InlinePractice component (F016's subject), and — critically — the live PracticeQuestionsTab component that the reviewer did not cite.

Finding F016 is accurate but narrower than the reviewer's use of it: it critiques InlinePractice (the embedded card inside the Learn Mode reading flow) specifically for lacking a write-and-self-mark loop — "No writing, no self-marking, no model answer" is F016's *impact* framing of that one component's UX limitation, not a factual claim that no model-answer content exists anywhere in the product. dismissed.quote: The 4 Macroeconomic Objectives — Edexcel IAL Economics WEC12 Notes
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I read both cited sources directly.

Spec (audit/raw/econ_spec.txt, section 2.3.6, "1 Macroeconomic objectives"): six sub-points a–f: growth, low/stable inflation, low unemployment, BoP equilibrium on current account, balanced government budget, greater income equality. Correct that the spec itself lists six.

Page body (page.js): repeatedly says "six main objectives" (line 301), "All six objectives" (line 308), and lists a Q&A giving all six (line 124). Also correct that the body says six throughout.

But the title's "4" is not a fabricated or arbitrary number — it names a real, widely-taught subset: "the four classic macroeconomic objectives" (growth, inflation, unemployment, balance of payments) is a standard framing in macroeconomics generally, independent of any one exam board, often distinguished from newer additions like income equality and environmental sustainability that modern specs (including this one) tack on. Crucially, the page does not hide this distinction — it states it explicitly and repeatedly right next to the "six" language:
- Line 157 (KEY_CONCEPTS card, user-visible on the page): "Six objectives, four classic" — "Growth, low inflation, low unemployment and BoP stability are the 'big four'. Income equality and environmental sustainability complete the modern set."
- Line 302 (body copy): "The four classic objectives are growth, low inflation, low unemployment and a sustainable balance of payments. Modern specifications add income equality and environmental sustainability. A strong WEC12 answer names all six..."
- Line 124 (FAQ answer): "The first four are the classic 'big four' — income equality and environmental sustainability are increasingly emphasised in modern exams."

So the "4" in the <title>/SEO metadata is the page's own established shorthand for the classic core (which it names, unprompted, three separate times in the visible body), not a contradiction of the "six" the page also states. This is the "right number under a different, reasonable, and page-consistent counting rule" scenario — closer to "Top 4" headline framing of a named subset within a fuller list than to a false factual claim. I also confirmed the visible on-page H1 (line 243, "Macroeconomic Objectives — every target, every trade-off") doesn't even assert a number at all — only the <title>/meta tag (SEO/SERP copy, which is metadata rather than primary body content and conventionally compresses) uses "4," and it does so by pointing at a real subset the page itself names "classic."

One side note for completeness, not part of the accusation being adjudicated: the body's own six-item "modern" list substitutes "environmental sustainability" for the spec's actual sixth item "balanced government budget," which is a separate potential accuracy issue in the body content — but that's not the claim under review (the reviewer's accusation is specifically about the title's "4" vs. the body's "six," not about which six items are named), so it doesn't change this verdict.

Given the explicit, repeated, user-visible reconciliation on the page itself, and the fact that "four macroeconomic objectives" is a legitimate, commonly used pedagogical framing (not an invented number), I find the title defensible as ordinary marketing/SEO shorthand for a named subset, not a false claim.

dismissed.quote: Free annotated model answers for Edexcel IAL Economics and Business exam questions.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
The reviewer's factual predicates check out in isolation: MODEL_ANSWERS is BASE_ANSWERS (28) + EXPANSION_ANSWERS (38) = 66 items, app/model-answers/page.js:68 does call <ModelAnswersPage answers={MODEL_ANSWERS} sectionsMeta={...} /> with no freeMode prop, ModelAnswersPage.jsx:253 defaults freeMode=false, and isLocked(index) at :284-289 does lock every index>0 for non-premium/signed-out visitors on that one hub route. So on /model-answers specifically, 1 of 66 answers is unlocked without a subscription. That much is accurate.

Where the accusation breaks down is scope. I grepped every use of the exact copy template "Free annotated model answers for Edexcel IAL ... exam questions" and every use of <ModelAnswersPage>. The identical claim (with topic-specific wording) is also the meta description on 22 other live, sitemapped pages — e.g. app/economics/demand-model-answers/page.js, app/business/marketing-mix-model-answers/page.js, and 20 more, all listed in app/sitemap.js at priority 0.8 and internally linked from topic pages (e.g. app/economics/aggregate-demand/page.js:123). Every one of those renders via components/SectionModelAnswersPage.jsx:56, which calls <ModelAnswersPage answers={sectionAnswers} freeMode={true} /> unconditionally — no auth check, no isPremium gate. With freeMode=true, isLocked() returns false for every index (ModelAnswersPage.jsx:286), so every model answer in that section is fully readable by anyone, signed in or not.

In other words: the same 66-answer dataset (data/modelAnswersData.js, filtered by section) is delivered completely free, with no login and no paywall, across 22 confirmed production routes carrying this exact marketing line. The /model-answers hub the reviewer cites is a convenience aggregator/browse-all view of that same content, where only the aggregated multi-topic browsing experience is metered (1 free sample, rest behind 'Unlock All' / sign-in) — plausibly a deliberate freemium pattern (sample the format, then either browse per-topic for free or pay for the all-in-one filterable hub), not a fabricated claim. The copy never asserts 'all 66 are free here' or 'no login required on this page' — it's a general descriptor of the content category, and it is literally true: free annotated model answers for Edexcel IAL Economics and Business exist on revvylearn.com, in volume, unconditionally. The reviewer's 'exactly one of 66' figure is only true when arbitrarily scoped to a single aggregator route and ignores the 22 sibling pages carrying the identical claim where it is 100% accurate. That is a misreading of ground truth, not a fabricated ad claim — and it is also ordinary freemium marketing language even taken at face value.

dismissed.quote: Free annotated model answers for Edexcel IAL Economics and Business. 4, 8 and 20-mark exam questions with mark scheme commentary.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
Verified the reviewer's cited source directly.

Confirmed facts:
- app/model-answers/page.js:17 (the OG description under review) feeds `ModelAnswersPage` without `freeMode` (line ~57 of page.js: `<ModelAnswersPage answers={MODEL_ANSWERS} sectionsMeta={MODEL_ANSWERS_SECTIONS} />`), so the paywall logic in ModelAnswersPage.jsx applies.
- ModelAnswersPage.jsx:284-291: `isLocked(index)` returns `index > 0` for non-premium, non-freeMode users — i.e., within whatever list is currently being displayed, item 0 is free and the rest are locked.
- Critically, `idx` (ModelAnswersPage.jsx:339, `filtered.map((answer, idx) => ...)`) is the index within `filtered`, the array AFTER the mark-filter is applied (ModelAnswersPage.jsx ~266-272), not the index within the full 66-item dataset. The "Filter by marks" bar (ModelAnswersPage.jsx ~312-329, buttons for 4/8/20 marks, generated from `markOptions` over the *unfiltered* full answer set) is rendered unconditionally, with no premium gate.
- Data check: data/modelAnswersData.js + data/modelAnswersExpansion.js together contain 66 answers (27 four-mark, 30 eight-mark, 9 twenty-mark), confirmed by direct count.

Consequence: a completely anonymous, non-paying visitor can click "4 marks", "8 marks", or "20 marks" in the filter bar and see one full, fully annotated, unlocked model answer — with mark scheme rows, PEEL grid, annotation legend, and examiner commentary — in EACH of those three categories, for free, with zero signup. That is exactly what the OG copy names: "Free annotated model answers ... 4, 8 and 20-mark exam questions with mark scheme commentary."

The reviewer's own framing — "the 'Free' claim that a visitor cannot act on" — is factually wrong: a visitor demonstrably CAN act on it, in exactly the three categories the copy calls out. The reviewer's "65 of 66 locked" statistic is arithmetically correct but only describes the default "All" filter view; it doesn't contradict the copy, because the copy never claims volume ("all", "every", "66", "unlimited") — it only claims a free tier exists across the three named mark-value categories, which is true.

This is also textbook OG/meta-description marketing compression (a search/social teaser, not a pricing disclosure), and "Free X, here are the categories" is standard freemium framing across ed-tech (one real free sample per tier, paid unlock for the rest) — not a quantifiable false assertion. PaywallOverlay.jsx's own copy ("Unlock ALL Model Answers", "Get Pro — £1 first month") is consistent with a genuine freemium structure, not a bait-and-switch with zero free access.

I do not find this indefensible. The reviewer appears to have read the aggregate lock ratio without noticing that the per-mark-value filter (4/8/20 — the exact breakdown the copy itself lists) each independently exposes one free unlocked example, which directly satisfies the specific claim made.

dismissed.quote: Annotated model answers for Edexcel International A-Level Economics and Business — 4, 8, and 20-mark questions with mark scheme breakdowns, PEEL structure, and examiner commentary.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I verified the reviewer's raw counts and they're correct — checked directly:

- data/modelAnswersData.js + data/modelAnswersExpansion.js: 66 total answer objects (28 + 38), 35 with a peel object / 31 with peel: null (16+15).
- components/ModelAnswersPage.jsx:45-46, PeelGrid: `if (!peel) return null;` — confirmed, no PEEL block renders for the 31 null entries.
- Line 310's SEO intro does say "PEEL structure (where applicable)" — confirmed.

But I cross-tabbed the null/non-null split against the `marks` field, which the reviewer's accusation doesn't mention, and it's the whole story:

  4-mark:  27 answers — 0 with PEEL, 27 null (100% null)
  8-mark:  30 answers — 26 with PEEL, 4 null (87% have PEEL)
  20-mark:  9 answers — 9 with PEEL, 0 null (100% have PEEL)

PEEL (Point-Evidence-Explain-Link) is a paragraph structure for extended, evaluative writing. It has no sensible application to a 4-mark knowledge/application question (typically a one- or two-sentence definition-plus-example, confirmed by reading the first BASE_ANSWERS entry — 'scarcity-opportunity-cost-4' is two short paragraphs, not an essay). It belongs, and is used, almost universally exactly where extended writing actually occurs: every 20-marker and the large majority of 8-markers. The 4 null 8-markers are outliers within that tier, not evidence the feature is broadly absent from where it should live.

I also checked whether the other two features in the same sentence ('mark scheme breakdowns', 'examiner commentary') are themselves unconditional, to see if the hero line is meant as a strict per-item AND across all three: markScheme (66/66) and examinerCommentary (66/66) are present on every single answer with no nulls. So two of the three listed features are in fact universal; only PEEL varies, and it varies for a principled pedagogical reason rather than being a gap in coverage.

Grammatically, 'X, Y, and Z questions with A, B, and C' in a hero headline is standard compressed marketing phrasing describing the collection's feature set (like 'ebooks, audiobooks, and courses with summaries, quizzes, and certificates') — it is not read by an ordinary visitor as a strict logical conjunction guaranteeing all three features identically on every one of 66 items, especially for a feature (PEEL) that is inherently tied to extended-response writing. The more granular, qualified phrasing in the on-page SEO paragraph ('PEEL structure (where applicable)') isn't a contradiction of the hero — it's the normal pattern of a punchy headline followed by more precise supporting copy, and both are user-visible so nothing is being hidden.

Given the feature is real, substantial (present across 100% of 20-mark and 87% of 8-mark answers, i.e. wherever extended writing occurs), correctly absent where it doesn't structurally apply, and the sentence is ordinary hero-copy shorthand rather than a per-item guarantee, I find this defensible. It is closer to a borderline phrasing choice than a false claim — worth tightening for extra safety, but not something that should be characterized to the founder as broken/false advertising.

dismissed.quote: Free notes for every spec point. Practice with flashcards, quizzes and AI tutor.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I read app/model-answers/page.js:97 and the cited source directly.

1. "Free notes for every spec point" — Verified independently true. StudyApp.jsx:24 puts 'notes' in FREE_TABS (no paywall gate at all — not even a preview cap like flashcards/quiz get). And per the reviewer's own cited audit (audit/raw/research-ial-spec-coverage.md:12-14), the top-level structural finding is: "Result: NONE missing. All 43 app sections map 1:1 onto the spec's numbered headings, in the correct order and with the correct IAL numbering." Every one of the 43 official Pearson spec headings (1.3.1-4.3.6 Econ, 1.3.1-4.3.4 Business) — which is what "spec point" naturally denotes in exam-prep marketing (a syllabus topic, e.g. "1.3.1 Nature of Economics") — has a free notes section. The gaps the audit found (3b renewable/non-renewable resources, 4c/4d capital vs consumer goods, 1.3.6 sub-topic 6 speculation/bubbles, 3.3.6 contingency planning, etc.) are missing lettered sub-bullets *within* covered spec points, not missing spec points. The audit itself frames this as "one level down" from spec-point coverage. "Notes for every spec point" reasonably and accurately describes point-level (heading-level) coverage; it does not promise word-for-word exhaustive coverage of every lettered sub-bullet a syllabus PDF lists, any more than "recipes for every meal of the day" promises every possible dish variant within breakfast.

2. "Practice with flashcards, quizzes and AI tutor" — The reviewer's central error is treating "Free" as governing this second sentence. It doesn't, grammatically or visually: these are two separate sentences ("Free notes for every spec point." / "Practice with flashcards, quizzes and AI tutor."). The word "Free" appears only in the first sentence and modifies only "notes." I confirmed via grep that the word "free" appears nowhere else near this copy, and nothing in the surrounding JSX (app/model-answers/page.js) or the CTA block extends "free" to the second sentence. The second sentence is a plain feature description — this is the standard freemium-landing-page pattern (lead with the free hook, then describe the fuller feature set you unlock, i.e. an upsell), not a factual claim that AI Tutor/flashcards/quizzes cost nothing. The app is internally consistent with this: it clearly labels these as 'PREMIUM — £1 FIRST MONTH' with padlocks (StudyApp.jsx:168-188) the moment a visitor actually opens them — there's no bait-and-switch since the CTA click-through ('Open Revvy Learn') leads straight into an interface that immediately and honestly discloses the paywall.

Given the grammatical separation holds up and the spec-point coverage claim holds up under the audit's own top-level finding, I could not honestly refute this as false advertising. Per the task's default-to-defensible instruction under genuine uncertainty about "spec point" granularity, and given the stronger clear-cut refutation on the "Practice with..." sentence, the copy stands as ordinary, accurate marketing language.

dismissed.quote: model opening sentences that hit top bands
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I opened both cited sources plus the surrounding context the reviewer didn't cite.

1. Location of the disputed copy: "model opening sentences that hit top bands" sits inside `metadata.description` at app/command-words/page.js:11 — an SEO `<meta name="description">` tag, not a string rendered in the page's visible body. The reviewer's own evidence (CommandWordsPage.jsx:26-40 rendering word/definition/examiner_expects/example) is accurate for that component, but a meta description is written to summarize the page's overall value proposition for a search-result snippet — it is not obligated to be a literal manifest of one child component's props, and it's ordinary practice for such copy to describe the broader resource the page belongs to.

2. The command-words page (app/command-words/page.js, lines ~85-93) explicitly renders a "Related resources" section directly beneath the command-word list, linking to `/model-answers`. That is not a stretch or a buried footer link — it's the page's own next section, one click away.

3. I opened /model-answers (app/model-answers/page.js) and its data source (data/modelAnswersData.js). That feature contains full annotated model answers — e.g. "Scarcity is the fundamental economic problem..." and "Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded..." — each answer's opening sentence is exactly the kind of top-band opener the copy describes. The examiner commentary repeatedly uses the literal phrase "top band" (confirmed 4 occurrences, e.g. "earning the application marks that push into the top band," "pushes the answer into the top band," "This answer reaches the top band by..."). So "model opening sentences that hit top bands" is a real, verifiable feature of the linked resource, not an invented claim.

4. The reviewer scoped their audit narrowly to the `command_words` table and CommandWordsPage.jsx's three fields, and concluded "no opening sentences exist anywhere in the feature." That's true of the isolated database row/component, but false of the page as a whole, which is what the meta description is describing and what a user experiencing this page (word list + explicitly promoted related resources) actually encounters.

This is a defensible case of an SEO/marketing description characterizing a hub page's full value (its own content plus its directly-linked companion resource) rather than one subcomponent's exact field list — ordinary practice, and factually grounded in real content that exists on the site and is linked from this exact page.

dismissed.quote: Complete guide to Edexcel IAL command words with example answers and mark breakdowns. Define, Explain, Analyse, Assess, Evaluate.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
The reviewer's strongest and most specific claim is factually wrong: examples DO exist. audit/raw/command_words.json has an `example` field populated for all 18 records (Define, State, Identify, Calculate, Draw, Outline, Describe, Explain, Analyse, Assess, Evaluate, Discuss, Distinguish, Compare, Justify, Suggest, "To what extent", Consider) — each one a real worked exam-style question with a model answer sketch (e.g. Calculate's example literally shows "PED = % change in Qd / % change in P = -20% / 10% = -2"). components/CommandWordsPage.jsx:33-38 renders `word.example` under a visible "Example" label whenever it exists. So the claim "there are no example answers... in the data or the component" is simply not true — this half of the reviewer's two-part accusation is a misread.

"Mark breakdowns" is thinner but not zero: examiner_expects mentions marks explicitly for 3/18 words (Define: "Usually worth 2 marks"; State: "Often worth 1 mark per point stated"; Draw: "Labels are essential for marks"), and several others describe what earns marks (formula/values/units for Calculate, etc.) without a numeric tally. It's not a rigorous per-word mark scheme, but a two-line OG snippet promising "mark breakdowns" is reasonably read by a visitor as "guidance on how marks are awarded," which the page does provide in prose form, not as a false "there is literally nothing about marks anywhere" claim.

On "complete" and the word list: the five words actually named in the copy — Define, Explain, Analyse, Assess, Evaluate — are all genuine Edexcel IAL command words, confirmed against Appendix 6 for Economics (research-ial-spec-coverage.md:137: Define, Explain, Analyse, Evaluate) and Business (line 152: Define, Explain, Analyse, Assess, Evaluate). Nothing false is asserted about any specific word named in the copy. The reviewer's deeper point — that the underlying data set omits Examine/Construct and includes ~9 words (State, Identify, Outline, Describe, Distinguish, Compare, Justify, Suggest, Consider) that aren't in either spec's official Appendix 6 tariff table — is a legitimate content-completeness note about the command_words table, but "Complete guide to X" is standard genre marketing language (like "The Complete Guide to Rome"), not a literal claim to match an appendix line-for-line, and it doesn't misstate any of the words it actually calls out by name.

This is OpenGraph description copy (app/command-words/page.js:15) — genuinely live and user-facing via social/link-preview cards, not a comment or dead code, so it does need to clear the bar, and on balance it does: the accusation's specific evidentiary claim (no examples anywhere) is demonstrably false, and the remaining claims are either partially true (some mark content exists) or ordinary marketing framing (complete guide) rather than a falsifiable factual misstatement about the five words actually named.

dismissed.quote: Example answers included
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I opened both cited sources directly.

app/command-words/page.js:66 renders "Example answers included" as one of three proof-stat chips in the hero (word count / example answers included / mark breakdowns). components/CommandWordsPage.jsx:33-38 renders each word's `example` field under a section labeled "Example" (singular, not "Example answer") — that part of the reviewer's citation is accurate.

But the claim that the `example` field is "never a written answer, only a question plus a one-line hint about how to approach it" does not hold up against the actual data in audit/raw/command_words.json (18 rows, all inspected). Several entries ARE the answer, not just method guidance, e.g.:
- Suggest: '"Suggest a reason why demand for cigarettes is price inelastic." — Addictive nature means consumers are unresponsive to price changes.' — that's the substantive answer, not a hint about approach.
- Justify: '"Justify the use of subsidies..." — Because marginal social benefit > marginal private benefit, subsidy closes the gap.' — again, the actual justification.
- Explain: '"Explain why a rise in income increases demand..." — Higher income → more purchasing power → consumers buy more → demand curve shifts right.' — a complete, if compact, explanatory chain (this is literally what an Explain answer needs: a causal chain).
- Distinguish, Compare, State, Calculate: each gives the concrete distinguishing facts / comparison points / named factors / worked numeric substitution (PED = -20%/10% = -2), i.e., real answer content, not merely "how to approach."

The reviewer's example (Define) is genuinely the weakest case — it does read as method guidance ("state the formula or a clear definition") rather than the definition itself — and a few others (Identify, Describe) lean toward approach-guidance since they reference a diagram/data not shown. But that's a subset, not the whole set, so "never a written answer" is an overstatement/misreading, not an accurate description of the dataset.

For the extended-writing words (Analyse/Assess/Evaluate/Discuss/To what extent), the example does compress the argument into a plan rather than full essay prose — but a compressed model-answer sketch showing the actual line of argument (not just "write an intro, then evaluate") is ordinary and reasonable to call an "example answer" in a revision-site context. No reasonable reader expects a hero-stat chip ("Example answers included") to promise full-length worked essays for every command word; it promises that each entry includes an example of what answering looks like, which is true for essentially all 18 rows.

Additionally, the "Example" UI label vs. "Example answers" marketing copy is the kind of compression that's completely standard between a compact card label and a hero proof-point; it doesn't misrepresent what's stored or rendered.

Given the actual content is real (question + genuine answer-bearing guidance) for the large majority of entries, and the copy is a short proof-stat rather than a precise technical claim, this is defensible ordinary marketing language, not a factual falsehood. Per the default-to-defensible instruction and because the reviewer's blanket "never a written answer" claim is contradicted by direct inspection of the source data, I'm marking this defensible.

dismissed.quote: Free notes for every spec point. Practice with exam-style questions and model answers.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I read the copy, the cited component, the model-answers route, and the audit file directly.

1) "Practice with exam-style questions and model answers" does not assert the model answers are free. The sentence is grammatically separate from "Free notes for every spec point." — "Free" modifies only "notes." Confirmed against ModelAnswersPage.jsx:284-289: only the first of each set is unlocked for non-premium (isLocked returns index>0 unless isPremium or freeMode), and app/model-answers/page.js doesn't pass freeMode, so 65/66 are gated for a signed-out visitor on that specific page — the reviewer's arithmetic is correct, but it doesn't make the copy false, because the copy never claims all model answers are free.

Crucially, this exact two-sentence pattern — "Free notes for every spec point. Practice with [X]." — recurs verbatim across the site with different X's: "Practice with flashcards, quizzes and AI tutor" (model-answers/page.js:97, past-papers, glossary), "Adaptive flashcards, practice questions and AI tutor unlock with Pro" (business/economics unit pages). Flashcards, quizzes and the AI tutor are also Pro-gated (confirmed by app/upgrade/page.js:130: "Every spec point is readable without an account. Pro is the practice, not the content."). So the whole site's established, consistent messaging convention is: content (notes) = free, practice features = the paid tier, named explicitly in the CTA without a "free" qualifier attached to them. The command-words page CTA is just one more instance of that same non-deceptive convention, not an isolated overreach.

2) "Free notes for every spec point": audit/raw/research-ial-spec-coverage.md Section 1 (lines ~14-20, above the reviewer's cited 57-62/68) states outright: "SPEC HEADINGS WITH NO SECTION... Result: NONE missing. All 43 app sections map 1:1 onto the spec's numbered headings, in the correct order and with the correct IAL numbering." The gaps the reviewer cites (merit/demerit goods, accelerator effect, missing sub-bullets like 3b/3d/4c/4d/5c) are sub-topic- and sub-bullet-level completeness gaps *within* covered spec-point sections, not missing spec points. "Notes for every spec point" is naturally read — and is used elsewhere on the site itself ("4 units · 24 spec points", "spec point by spec point") — at the heading/topic granularity, where coverage is 100%. Reading it instead as a guarantee of zero omissions at the lettered-sub-bullet level is a stricter interpretation than the phrase, or ordinary usage of "covers every topic," supports.

Net: the copy is accurate on its natural reading and consistent with how identical phrasing is used sitewide. This is ordinary, defensible freemium marketing language, not a factual misstatement.

dismissed.quote: Free notes for every spec point. Test your knowledge with flashcards and quizzes.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
Checked both prongs of the accusation against the actual code and the audit the reviewer cites.

1) "Free notes for every spec point." The audit file itself (audit/raw/research-ial-spec-coverage.md, section 1) states: "SPEC HEADINGS WITH NO SECTION (top-level x.3.x headings) — Result: NONE missing. All 43 app sections map 1:1 onto the spec's numbered headings, in the correct order and with the correct IAL numbering." In exam-revision usage, "spec point" ordinarily refers to these numbered headings (1.3.1, 1.3.5, 2.3.2, etc.) — the units students and teachers actually call "spec points" — not every individual lettered sub-bullet inside a heading. Under that standard, entirely reasonable reading, the claim is literally true: there is a free notes section for every spec point, 43/43. The gaps the reviewer cites (missing sub-bullets like 3b/4c/5c inside 1.3.1, the absent "Speculation and market bubbles" sub-topic, off-spec GCE leftovers, etc.) are one level down — sub-topic/sub-bullet depth, not "spec point" existence — which is a completeness-of-depth issue, not a fabricated point ("we have a page for a topic that doesn't exist"). Marketing copy claiming coverage of "every spec point" is standard shorthand for syllabus breadth, not a warranty of zero omissions at the most granular sub-bullet level, and the cited audit's own top-level finding supports the copy rather than contradicting it.

2) "Test your knowledge with flashcards and quizzes." The word "Free" in the sentence grammatically modifies "notes," not this second sentence. The second sentence makes no free/unlimited claim — it just says the activity (testing knowledge via flashcards/quizzes) exists, which is true: free users genuinely get real flashcards and real quiz questions (FlashcardsTab.jsx PREVIEW_LIMIT=2, QuizTab.jsx PREVIEW_LIMIT=2) before hitting a paywall card. This isn't a fake teaser or dark pattern — StudyApp.jsx shows the premium/free split is disclosed immediately and clearly in-app: the section overview renders an explicit "PREMIUM — £1 FIRST MONTH" header with padlock icons over the Flashcards/Quiz/Tutor cards for non-premium users (StudyApp.jsx:168,172-182), and PREVIEW_TABS (line 27) intentionally shows a real preview before a full paywall — there's no attempt to hide the gating. A visitor who clicks through from this CTA sees the premium label within one click, before any purchase or commitment. This is ordinary freemium marketing practice (lead with the free hook, describe the fuller feature set, disclose tiering in-product) — not a false "everything is free" assertion, since the copy never says "free flashcards" or "unlimited quizzes."

The reviewer conflates (a) "spec point" with the finer-grained sub-bullet audit findings, and (b) a general feature description with an implicit-but-unstated "free" claim that the sentence doesn't actually make and that the in-app UX doesn't contradict (gating is disclosed immediately, not concealed). Both readings the reviewer relies on are less natural than the ones the copy and code actually support, so the accusation does not hold up as a factual falsehood.

dismissed.quote: Use flashcards, quizzes and the AI tutor alongside these guides.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I opened all cited sources directly.

Verified facts (reviewer is right on these): PREMIUM_TABS = new Set(['mistakes','tutor']) (StudyApp.jsx:28) gets a full-block paywall with zero preview (StudyApp.jsx:671-674: `if (PREMIUM_TABS.has(activeTab) && !isPremium) return <PaywallOverlay .../>`). FlashcardsTab.jsx:13 and QuizTab.jsx:15 both set PREVIEW_LIMIT = 2, and free users are shown a paywall after item 2 (FlashcardsTab.jsx:214-220, QuizTab.jsx:169-172). isPremium requires an active paid (or lifetime) subscription (lib/entitlements.js:18-37) — there's no cardless-trial path that grants it, so this isn't mitigated by a free-trial window.

Where the accusation overreaches: the disputed sentence is "Use flashcards, quizzes and the AI tutor alongside these guides" — a CTA verb inviting exploration, not a claim of "free," "unlimited," or "full access." It doesn't quantify anything the preview limits could contradict. For flashcards and quizzes, the claim is literally true: a free reader can use them (2 real cards / 2 real questions), which is exactly the kind of freemium teaser this phrasing describes across the industry (Quizlet, Duolingo, etc. all pitch premium-gated features in top-of-funnel marketing copy without a paywall disclaimer inline). Once a reader actually follows the CTA, the app is not deceptive about it — SectionOverview shows explicit "PREMIUM — £1 FIRST MONTH" labels with padlock icons on Flashcards/Quiz/Tutor cards before any interaction (StudyApp.jsx:167-188), and PaywallOverlay lists the premium feature set and price up front. There's no dark pattern, no hidden charge, no bait past a point of commitment.

I also checked the surrounding page copy for a conflation the reviewer didn't cite: the hero explicitly scopes the "100% free" claim to the guides themselves ("X Economics guides / Y Business guides / 100% free", app/guides/page.js ~line 39), separately from the later "Start revising interactively" CTA that names flashcards/quiz/tutor without repeating "free." That structure (free core content + an unqualified upsell CTA to premium tools) is standard and actually cuts against the "no hint of a paywall" framing being deceptive — the page never claims these three tools are free; it only claims the guides are.

The AI Tutor is the closest thing to a real problem: a free reader truly cannot "use" it at all (zero preview), which is a harder gap than flashcards/quiz's partial-use case. That's worth noting to the team, but a single imperative CTA verb naming a premium feature alongside two partially-free ones is ordinary marketing shorthand for "here's what the platform offers," not a factual warranty of unrestricted access to each named item — and disclosure happens honestly one click later, before any payment. Given the instruction to default to defensible when genuinely uncertain, and because no explicit "free"/"unlimited" claim is made in the disputed sentence, I'd keep this live rather than have it flow into a copy rewrite as a "false claim" finding.

dismissed.quote: Flashcards, quizzes, AI tutor & progress tracking for this topic
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I opened every cited file. The reviewer's individual factual claims about the codebase are accurate: - PREMIUM_TABS = new Set(['mistakes', 'tutor']) (components/StudyApp.jsx:27) with the comment "Full paywall block (no preview)" — confirmed at StudyApp.jsx:673-675 (renderTab: `if (PREMIUM_TABS.has(activeTab) && !isPremium) return `). The Tutor tab genuinely has zero free access. - QuizTab.jsx:15 and FlashcardsTab.jsx:13 both set `PREVIEW_LIMIT = 2`, applied via `isPreview = PREVIEW_TABS.has(activeTab) && !isPremium` (StudyApp.jsx:687, 735-736). Confirmed. - F001 and F027 in audit/ledger.json are real, open, critical/medium findings: completion flags, review schedule ("strength"/spacing) are written only to localStorage in LearnModeTab.jsx's `handleComplete`, never to the server. Confirmed. - app/guides/[slug]/page.js:94 does read `href={`/${guide.subject}`}` — the CTA goes to the subject hub (/economics or /business), not a specific topic/section. However, the piece I was asked to defend is specifically the copy string at line 92: "Flashcards, quizzes, AI tutor & progress tracking for this topic." Judged as marketing text (not as a spec of exact entitlements), it holds up: 1. It is a feature-list, not a quantitative or "free/unlimited" claim. It never says "free," "unlimited," "instant," or "syncs across devices." All four named features (flashcards, quizzes, AI tutor, progress tracking) genuinely exist in the app for every topic — none are fabricated or vaporware. 2. Freemium gating (2-item previews, full paywall on Tutor) is disclosed at the point of use inside the product itself — lock icons and a "PREMIUM — £1 FIRST MONTH" label are rendered directly on the tab cards (StudyApp.jsx:172-188). Naming a premium capability in a top-of-funnel feature list without asterisking its tier is standard, ubiquitous SaaS/edtech marketing practice (Notion AI, Duolingo Max, etc. all do this) and is not typically treated as a factual falsehood. 3. "Progress tracking" is not entirely broken across devices, which is actually a place the reviewer overstates the case: `furthest_step` (which section/step a logged-in user is on) *is* persisted server-side via /api/progress/content (GET/POST, keyed on user_id) and `readSavedStep` prefers the DB value over localStorage (StudyApp.jsx:407-413). What doesn't survive a device change is the richer spaced-repetition state (completion flag, strength, 1/3/7/14-day review schedule) per F001/F027 — a real and serious gap, but narrower than "progress tracking does not survive a device change" as a blanket statement about the feature named in the copy. 4. The button's destination (/${guide.subject}, not the specific topic) is a genuine, separately-located bug (line 94, a ``, not the `

` copy on line 92). It's a legitimate routing/UX defect worth fixing, but it isn't itself false text in the sentence I was asked to defend — the sentence doesn't claim "clicking takes you straight into this exact topic's tools," only that the app has these capabilities for this topic. Given genuine uncertainty about where "standard freemium feature-listing" ends and "misleading" begins, and the instruction to default to defensible when uncertain, I'm calling this defensible. That said, the underlying product gaps are real and worth flagging on their own: (a) Tutor has literally no free preview unlike the other two gated features, and (b) the CTA link target doesn't match "this topic." I'd route those as separate product/UX bugs (audit F001/F027 already track the progress-sync issue; the href mismatch at page.js:94 is undocumented and worth its own ticket) rather than as grounds to rewrite this specific line of marketing copy. That's why I corrected severity down to medium rather than accepting the implied high/critical false-advertising framing — real issues exist nearby, but the quoted sentence itself is ordinary, defensible marketing language.

dismissed.quote: Use flashcards, quizzes and the AI tutor to nail your understanding.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
Verified the reviewer's mechanics claims are accurate — StudyApp.jsx:27 puts 'tutor' in PREMIUM_TABS ("Full paywall block (no preview)"), and renderTab() (line ~670) shows a full PaywallOverlay for any PREMIUM_TABS user who isn't subscribed, with zero free access. FlashcardsTab.jsx:13 and QuizTab.jsx:15 do both set PREVIEW_LIMIT = 2. So the reviewer read the code correctly.

But the copy itself makes no claim about price or access tier. "Use flashcards, quizzes and the AI tutor to nail your understanding" is a feature-naming, action-oriented CTA — it asserts that the app contains these three tools and that using them helps you learn, both of which are true. It never says "free," "included," "unlimited," or anything about cost. I checked app/guides/[slug]/page.js and found no adjacent free/price claim that would combine with this line to create a false overall impression (the only nearby "free" reference is unrelated schema.org `isAccessibleForFree: true` JSON-LD about the guide article itself). I also grepped the repo for "sign up free / free trial / start free" near CTAs and found none feeding into this page.

Notably, the codebase already has an explicit, deliberate house convention about exactly this tension: components/BackToApp.jsx's docstring says CTA copy should name "the next study action instead of the product ('Mark it against the model answers,' not 'Start your free trial')." The line under review follows that same pattern — it names the study action (use these tools to nail your understanding), not a commercial promise. Inside the actual app, the paywall is disclosed immediately and unambiguously (Padlock icons, a "PREMIUM — £1 FIRST MONTH" section header at StudyApp.jsx:167, and an instant PaywallOverlay for Tutor), so no one is misled past the point of commitment.

The reviewer's real objection — "the CTA doesn't disclose which named features are premium" — is a disclosure/UX preference, not a falsity. Feature lists on marketing/content pages routinely name capabilities without a paywall asterisk on each one; that's standard freemium practice, not deceptive advertising, especially when (as here) the product's own onboarding surfaces the paywall immediately and transparently. Nothing in the cited lines shows the copy is factually wrong or reproduces non-user-visible text — it's live, shipped copy describing real, existing product features.

dismissed.quote: Interactive visual map showing how Edexcel IAL Economics topics connect across micro and macro units.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
Checked the cited ground truth directly. topicLinksData.js:140-143 confirms UNITS = {1: UNIT_1, 2: UNIT_2} — i.e. exactly two datasets, one per unit, and each unit's `edges` array only ever references node ids that live inside that same unit's `nodes` array (verified by inspection of UNIT_1.edges lines 44-75 and UNIT_2.edges lines 103-137 — no edge has a `from`/`to` pair spanning the two id sets). TopicLinksPage.jsx:68-81 confirms the UI toggles between "Unit 1: Microeconomics" and "Unit 2: Macroeconomics" as two separate single-unit views (activeUnit state selects unitData = UNITS[activeUnit]) — you never see both graphs at once, and there is no rendered line crossing from a micro node to a macro node. So the reviewer's factual premises (no literal cross-unit edge; only two units of data exist) are correct as stated.

Where the accusation fails is in what the copy actually asserts. "Interactive visual map showing how Edexcel IAL Economics topics connect across micro and macro units" has its verb ("connect") take "topics" as subject; "across micro and macro units" most naturally scopes the map's *coverage* (it spans both the micro branch, Unit 1, and the macro branch, Unit 2 — which the UI itself labels exactly that way), not a promise that a specific edge crosses the micro/macro boundary. Under that ordinary reading, both component claims are literally true: (1) topics do connect — UNIT_1 has 30 edges across 20 nodes and UNIT_2 has 34 edges across 21 nodes, a genuinely dense linkage map with real "how X leads to Y" descriptions; (2) the map's coverage does span micro and macro — Unit 1 and Unit 2 are exactly the microeconomics and macroeconomics halves of the IAL spec, named as such in the product's own toggle buttons.

Critically, there is no bait-and-switch for a user: the product's own UI immediately tells you it is two separate, unit-scoped graphs ("Unit 1: Microeconomics" / "Unit 2: Macroeconomics" tabs), so nobody reading "connect... across micro and macro units" and then using the tool would feel misled into expecting a single unified cross-branch graph — what they get matches what a plain reading promises. The stronger reading the reviewer assumes (that the copy specifically guarantees edges *crossing* between micro and macro topics) is a possible but not the more natural parse, and is exactly the kind of ordinary, slightly-loose marketing phrasing ("connect across categories/units") that doesn't rise to a factual misrepresentation. Given genuine two-sided ambiguity and that the underlying facts (real connectivity, real micro+macro coverage) are true either way, I default to defensible.

dismissed.quote: Section 2.1 — Annotated model answers for sources of finance, venture capital, and start-up funding decisions.
dismissed.whyDismissed: The reviewer is right that the Pearson IAL spec code for this topic is 2.3.1 (confirmed in audit/raw/bus_spec.txt:844 and section-index.json's 'planning-raising-finance' entry), and that GCE-style short numbers like '2.1' don't appear in the IAL spec document. But the cited copy's 'Section 2.1' isn't a citation of the Pearson spec code at all — it's Revvy Learn's own internal section label. Every one of the 10 Business model-answers pages uses this same shortened unit.position scheme (1.1-1.5 for Unit 1, 2.1-2.5 for Unit 2), consistently mapping 1:1 in order onto the real spec numbers (1.3.1-1.3.5, 2.3.1-2.3.5). This isn't a one-off typo bleeding in from GCE; it's baked into data/modelAnswersData.js itself, where the underlying answer records are tagged sectionNumber: '2.1', and SectionModelAnswersPage.jsx uses that purely as an internal filter key. The functional link is correct too: sectionId='planning-raising-finance' matches the canonical id in section-index.json (whose real number is 2.3.1), so the page resolves to the right topic. The described content (sources of finance, venture capital, start-up/business-plan funding) matches spec 2.3.1's actual bullet points verbatim. Nothing in the quoted string claims to be quoting the exam board's numbering — a reasonable reader takes 'Section 2.1' as this site's own organizational label, the same way a textbook might renumber a syllabus's topics for its own chapter structure. Economics pages, by contrast, do mirror the full spec numbers exactly, showing Business intentionally chose a different, shorter house convention rather than confusing GCE and IAL. The one real wrinkle is that app/business/unit-2/page.js:16 labels the same topic 'ref: 2.3.1' on the hub page, creating a genuine internal inconsistency between two site pages — worth a follow-up cleanup ticket, but that's a polish/consistency issue, not evidence that this specific copy makes a false claim.

dismissed.quote: Interactive notes with diagrams, flashcards, quizzes and AI tutor.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I read both cited files plus the file the accused line lives in, all the way through the page body — and the reviewer only checked half the evidence.

What StudyApp.jsx/PaywallOverlay.jsx show is accurate as far as it goes: FREE_TABS = learn-mode, content, notes, diagrams, practice; PREVIEW_TABS (partial free preview, then paywall) = flashcards, quiz, extras; PREMIUM_TABS (full block, no preview) = mistakes, tutor. So flashcards and quizzes do have some genuine free interactive content; the AI tutor has none.

But the accused string is metadata.description on app/economics/page.js:9 — a search-engine/OG summary tag, not body copy — and it reads as two separate sentences: "Free Edexcel IAL Economics revision notes for all units: [WEC11–14]." followed by "Interactive notes with diagrams, flashcards, quizzes and AI tutor." The word "Free" grammatically modifies only the notes; the second sentence is a feature inventory (which is factually true — the product does have all of those things), not a repeated pricing claim.

More decisively, the page this metadata describes discloses the free/premium split explicitly and repeatedly in its own visible body copy, a few sections down:
- Line 292: "Notes are free. Flashcards, quizzes and AI tutor unlock with a subscription."
- Lines 296–330: a "What's included" grid tagging each feature card individually — Structured Notes "Free", Adaptive Flashcards "Premium", Practice Questions "Free", AI Tutor "Premium", Progress Tracking "Premium", Topic Links Map "Free".
- Line 408: "Free notes for every spec point. Adaptive flashcards, quizzes and AI tutor unlock with Pro — £1 for your first month."

So the same page that carries the "wrong" meta description is scrupulously transparent, multiple times, in plain English, about exactly which features are free and which are paid — including naming flashcards/quizzes/AI tutor as premium by name. Nobody who reaches the page is deceived; the disclosure is immediate and unambiguous. That's the opposite of a bait-and-switch. Separately, at ~250 characters the line-9 description is roughly 100 characters past Google's typical SERP truncation point, so the "flashcards, quizzes and AI tutor" clause likely doesn't even render in search results for most queries (the shorter openGraph.description at line 13 is the one that actually displays in social unfurls, and it's not the line the reviewer cited).

This is the standard, defensible freemium pattern: an SEO summary describes the full breadth of the product; on-page copy — right there on the same page — discloses the pricing tiers plainly. The reviewer cited the paywall implementation but never checked whether the page itself discloses the paywall, and it does, thoroughly. I don't think this rises to false or misleading; it reads as ordinary marketing/SEO shorthand backed by immediate, honest disclosure.

dismissed.quote: Interactive notes, flashcards, 20-mark essay guides, past paper practice and AI tutor.
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I read app/business/page.js:9, components/StudyApp.jsx:26-40, components/PaywallOverlay.jsx, app/past-papers/page.js, components/ExtrasTab.jsx, components/PracticeQuestionsTab.jsx, data/modelAnswersData.js, seed/seed-business-practice.mjs (which imports business-practice-unit1..4.mjs), and app/business/managing-finance-model-answers/page.js.

The reviewer's factual citations check out individually (flashcards and extras are PREVIEW_TABS = preview-then-paywall; tutor is a PREMIUM_TABS full block; /past-papers metadata literally says 'for Unit 1: WEC11 (Economics) and WBS11 (Business)'). But the accusation that this makes the copy false is a misreading on two counts:

1. Grammar of the sentence. 'Free Edexcel IAL Business revision notes for all units: [WBS11-14]. Interactive notes, flashcards, 20-mark essay guides, past paper practice and AI tutor.' is two sentences. 'Free' modifies 'revision notes' in sentence one; sentence two is a plain enumeration of platform features, not a repeated 'free' claim. It never says 'free flashcards' or 'free AI tutor.' Listing premium/freemium features alongside a genuinely free core product (notes) in an SEO meta description is standard freemium ed-tech copy (Quizlet, SaveMyExams, etc. do the same) — a feature existing behind a preview-then-paywall is not the same as the feature not existing, so 'flashcards ... and AI tutor' isn't a false statement, just an incomplete one about pricing tiers that the meta description was never trying to itemize.

2. '20-mark essay guides' is not exclusively the paywalled Extras tab. The reviewer only checked StudyApp.jsx's 'extras' tab (Chains of Analysis / Evaluation Points, paywalled). They missed the separate, fully free Model Answers pages (e.g. app/business/managing-finance-model-answers/page.js, metadata: 'Free annotated model answers...with mark scheme breakdowns and examiner commentary'), which data/modelAnswersData.js confirms include 20-mark entries, and which are linked directly from the always-free Practice tab (PracticeQuestionsTab.jsx, 'practice' is in FREE_TABS). That is a legitimate, and arguably the primary, referent for '20-mark essay guides,' and it is free with no login/paywall gate in SectionModelAnswersPage.jsx.

'Past paper practice' is the one genuinely soft spot: the dedicated /past-papers PDF-download feature is Unit-1-only sitewide by the product's own admission, while the business page covers Units 1-4. However, seed/seed-business-practice.mjs shows the free Practice tab has real exam-style, mark-scheme-graded questions (4/6/10/20 marks) across all four business units (unit1-4 practice files), which is a reasonable reading of 'past paper practice' distinct from literal PDF downloads. Given a defensible alternate reading exists and the instruction to default to defensible=true under genuine uncertainty, I don't think this single phrase makes the whole line false advertising, though the underlying product team may want to eventually expand past-paper PDFs beyond Unit 1 or use a more literal term on the dedicated past-papers page.

Net: this is ordinary marketing shorthand for a freemium product's feature set, not a specific, checkable false claim. I could not query the live Supabase content directly (read-only, no credentials), so this rests on the code/metadata evidence above, which is internally consistent and supports the defense.

dismissed.quote: Free notes, flashcards, past papers and model answers for IAL Economics (WEC11–WEC14) and Business (WBS11–WBS14).
dismissed.whyDismissed:
I read all four cited files plus the actual gating logic behind them.

components/StudyApp.jsx defines three tiers, not two:
- FREE_TABS (line 26): learn-mode, content, notes, diagrams, practice — fully unrestricted.
- PREVIEW_TABS (line 27): flashcards, quiz, extras — "Show preview then full paywall card." isPreview is computed purely from `!isPremium` (line 686), with no login required.
- PREMIUM_TABS (line 28): mistakes, tutor only — zero preview, hard PaywallOverlay immediately (line 671-674).

The reviewer cites StudyApp.jsx:36, where flashcards carries `premium: true` in the tab-metadata array. But that flag only drives which tab shows a lock badge / which set it belongs to — it is not the same as "premium: true" meaning "fully inaccessible without paying." Flashcards sits in PREVIEW_TABS, the softer tier, not PREMIUM_TABS.

I then opened components/FlashcardsTab.jsx directly: `PREVIEW_LIMIT = 2` (line 13), and non-premium users get a real, functioning flashcard experience — flip, mark got-it/review, deck logic — for the first 2 cards of every section, with no sign-up or payment required, before hitting PaywallOverlay (line 207-213, "You've previewed 2 of N flashcards"). This is a genuine free tier, not a comment, dead code, or unreachable path.

The reviewer's implicit baseline — that notes, past papers and model answers are unconditionally free while flashcards uniquely are not — doesn't hold up either. I checked components/ModelAnswersPage.jsx:284-287: "First answer is free; rest locked for non-premium," and app/model-answers/page.js (the main hub) renders it with the default `freeMode=false`, so model answers on the actual site are gated exactly the same way flashcards are (one free sample, then paywall) — arguably more restrictive (1 free item vs. 2 full cards). Only notes (FREE_TABS) and past papers (app/past-papers/page.js, components/PastPapersPage.jsx — no PaywallOverlay import anywhere in that file) are unconditionally free with no cap.

So the accurate picture is: notes and past papers are fully unrestricted; flashcards and model answers both offer a real, working free sample before a paywall. The landing copy's "Free notes, flashcards, past papers and model answers" is describing four resource categories each of which has a genuinely free, usable component — which is standard freemium/ed-tech marketing shorthand (Quizlet, Duolingo, etc. use identical framing for capped-free features), not a specific quantitative claim of "unlimited flashcards." components/PaywallOverlay.jsx:7-13 ("Interactive Flashcards" as a premium feature bullet) is consistent with this: the *unlimited/full* flashcard experience is the paid upsell, while a real free preview exists — the two aren't contradictory, they describe the freemium boundary from two different marketing surfaces.

Given a genuine, non-fabricated free tier exists for flashcards, and the reviewer's own implied comparison set (model answers) turns out to be gated in the same way, I don't think this rises to a false claim. It's ordinary marketing language for a freemium product, and the specific `premium: true` line cited is a UI/tier flag being over-read as an absolute paywall.

dismissed.quote: Free notes, flashcards, past papers and model answers for IAL Economics (WEC11–WEC14) and Business (WBS11–WBS14).
dismissed.whyDismissed:
The reviewer's citation is real but incomplete, and it doesn't establish the accusation. StudyApp.jsx:36 (`{ id: 'flashcards', label: 'Flashcards', Icon: CardsBlank, premium: true }`) does gate ONE flashcards surface: the "Flashcards" tab embedded in a specific section's in-app study dashboard. That tab shows only 2 preview cards (FlashcardsTab.jsx, PREVIEW_LIMIT=2) before rendering PaywallOverlay (components/PaywallOverlay.jsx), which the reviewer also cited.

But that is not the only, or even the primary, "flashcards" feature on the site.
